nodes.statement_short: Corollary's assumptions give Theorem 2's with gamma = gamma-bar and p, q swapped.

nodes.name: Upper embedding into G(n1,n2,m-bar)
nodes.statement: Note also that \[ m = \lceil(1-\bar\gamma)qN\rceil =\lceil N-pN-\bar\gamma q N\rceil= N - \lfloor(p+\bar\gamma q)N\rfloor=N-\bar m. \] Thus, by Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}, with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$ we have $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,N - \bar m) \subseteq \mathbb R(n_1,n_2,q)$, which, by taking complements, translates into~\eqref{eq_inverse_embed}.
nodes.statement_short: Since m = N - m-bar, Theorem 2 for the complement gives eq_inverse_embed.

nodes.name: Upper embedding into G(n1,n2,p'')
nodes.statement: Similarly \[ p' = (1 - 2\bar \gamma)q N = N - (p + 2\bar \gamma q) N = N - p'' N. \] Thus, by Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}, with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$ we have $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,N-p''N) \subseteq \mathbb R(n_1,n_2,q)$, which, by taking complements yields embedding~\eqref{eq:inverse_Gnp}.
nodes.statement_short: Same complement argument for the binomial version.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: We apply Theorem~\ref{thm_embed} and Corollary \ref{cor_embed} with $C=1$ and the corresponding~$C^*$. Note that for $n_1=n_2=n$, the ratio in~\eqref{eq_defI} equals $4/\log N = 2/\log n$, so \begin{equation} \mathbb I=1\quad\text{ if and only if }\quad\hat p<2/\log n. \end{equation} To prove~\eqref{eq:1stemb}, assume $p\gg\log n/n$ and $q \gg \left( \log n/n \right)^{1/4}$ and apply Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}. Note that condition~\eqref{eq:thm_embed_q} holds and it is straightforward to check that, regardless of whether $p \le 0.49$ or $p > 0.49$, $\gamma \to 0$. In particular, $\gamma \le 1/2$. We conclude that, indeed, embedding~\eqref{eq:1stemb} holds with $m = \lceil (1 - \gamma)p N \rceil \sim pn^2$ and~\eqref{eq:1stemb} still holds if we replace $\mathbb G(n,n,m)$ by $\mathbb G(n,n,p')$ with $p' = (1 - 2\gamma)p \sim p$. For~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} first note that when $p \to 1$, embedding~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} holds trivially with $m = n^2$ (even though a nontrivial embedding follows in this case under an additional assumption $q \gg \log n/n$. Hence, we further assume $q = \Omega(1)$, $p\gg\left(\log^3 n / n\right)^{1/4}$ and apply Corollary~\ref{cor_embed}. Note that condition~\eqref{eq:cor_embed_q} holds. It is routine to check, taking into account~\eqref{I=1}, that $\bar\gamma\le 1/2$ and, moreover, $\bar\gamma q = o(p)$. We conclude that~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} holds with $m = \lfloor(p + \bar\gamma q)N \rfloor \sim Np = n^2p$ and~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} still holds if $\mathbb G(n,n,m)$ is replaced by $\mathbb G(n,n,p')$ with $p' = p + 2 \bar \gamma q \sim p$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 to n1=n2=n with C=1 and check the error terms tend to 0.

nodes.name: Specialize with C=1 and balanced sides
nodes.statement: We apply Theorem~\ref{thm_embed} and Corollary \ref{cor_embed} with $C=1$ and the corresponding~$C^*$. Note that for $n_1=n_2=n$, the ratio in~\eqref{eq_defI} equals $4/\log N = 2/\log n$, so \begin{equation} \mathbb I=1\quad\text{ if and only if }\quad\hat p<2/\log n. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 with C=1; for n1=n2, I=1 iff p-hat < 2/log n.

nodes.name: I=1 iff p-hat < 2/log n (balanced case)
nodes.statement: \mathbb I=1\quad\text{ if and only if }\quad\hat p<2/\log n.
nodes.label: I=1

nodes.name: Lower embedding
nodes.statement: To prove~\eqref{eq:1stemb}, assume $p\gg\log n/n$ and $q \gg \left( \log n/n \right)^{1/4}$ and apply Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}. Note that condition~\eqref{eq:thm_embed_q} holds and it is straightforward to check that, regardless of whether $p \le 0.49$ or $p > 0.49$, $\gamma \to 0$. In particular, $\gamma \le 1/2$. We conclude that, indeed, embedding~\eqref{eq:1stemb} holds with $m = \lceil (1 - \gamma)p N \rceil \sim pn^2$ and~\eqref{eq:1stemb} still holds if we replace $\mathbb G(n,n,m)$ by $\mathbb G(n,n,p')$ with $p' = (1 - 2\gamma)p \sim p$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2's conditions hold and gamma -> 0, giving the lower embedding.

nodes.name: Upper embedding
nodes.statement: For~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} first note that when $p \to 1$, embedding~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} holds trivially with $m = n^2$ (even though a nontrivial embedding follows in this case under an additional assumption $q \gg \log n/n$. Hence, we further assume $q = \Omega(1)$, $p\gg\left(\log^3 n / n\right)^{1/4}$ and apply Corollary~\ref{cor_embed}. Note that condition~\eqref{eq:cor_embed_q} holds. It is routine to check, taking into account~\eqref{I=1}, that $\bar\gamma\le 1/2$ and, moreover, $\bar\gamma q = o(p)$. We conclude that~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} holds with $m = \lfloor(p + \bar\gamma q)N \rfloor \sim Np = n^2p$ and~\eqref{eq:2ndemb} still holds if $\mathbb G(n,n,m)$ is replaced by $\mathbb G(n,n,p')$ with $p' = p + 2 \bar \gamma q \sim p$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial if p -> 1; otherwise Corollary 3 with gamma-bar q = o(p).

nodes.name: Number of edges M = pN
nodes.statement: Recall that \[ d_1 = pn_2\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_2 = pn_1 \] are the degrees of vertices in a $p$-biregular graph, and thus, the number of edges in any $p$-biregular graph $H \in {\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)$ is \[ M:=pN\qquad\text{where}\qquad N=n_1n_2. \]

nodes.name: Shorthand notation q, p-hat, n-hat, [n]
nodes.statement: Throughout the proofs we also use shorthand notation \begin{equation} q = 1 - p, \quad \hat p = \min \left\{ p, q \right\}, \quad \hat n = \min \left\{ n_1,n_2 \right\}, \end{equation} and $[n] := \left\{ 1, \dots, n \right\}$.

nodes.name: Shorthand q, p-hat, n-hat
nodes.statement: q = 1 - p, \quad \hat p = \min \left\{ p, q \right\}, \quad \hat n = \min \left\{ n_1,n_2 \right\},
nodes.label: eq_not

nodes.name: Neighborhood Gamma_G(v)
nodes.statement: By $\Gamma_{G}(v)$ we denote the set of neighbors of a vertex $v$ in a graph $G$.

nodes.name: Switching technique: auxiliary graph B and forward switching
nodes.statement: The switching technique is used to compare the size of two classes of graphs, say ${\mathcal{R}}$ and ${\mathcal{R}}'$, by defining an auxiliary bipartite graph $B:=B({\mathcal{R}},{\mathcal{R}}')$, in which two graphs $H \in {\mathcal{R}}$, $H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'$ are connected by an edge whenever $H$ can be transformed into $H'$ by some operation (a \emph{forward switching}) that deletes and/or creates some edges of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Switching graph B(R,R') joins H in R to H' in R' when a forward switching (edge deletions/insertions) turns H into H'.

nodes.name: Switching double-counting bounds
nodes.statement: By counting the number of edges of $B({\mathcal{R}},{\mathcal{R}}')$ in two ways, we see that \begin{equation} \sum_{H\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H) = \sum_{H'\in{\mathcal{R}}'}\deg_B(H'), \end{equation} which easily implies that \begin{equation} \frac{\min_{H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'} \deg_B(H')}{\max_{H \in {\mathcal{R}}} \deg_B(H)} \le \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|} \le \frac{\max_{H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'} \deg_B(H')}{\min_{H \in {\mathcal{R}}} \deg_B(H)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Double counting edges of B gives |R|/|R'| between ratios of extreme degrees in B.

nodes.name: Double counting edges of switching graph
nodes.statement: \sum_{H\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H) = \sum_{H'\in{\mathcal{R}}'}\deg_B(H'),
nodes.label: eq_BRR

nodes.name: Switching ratio bounds via min/max degrees
nodes.statement: \frac{\min_{H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'} \deg_B(H')}{\max_{H \in {\mathcal{R}}} \deg_B(H)} \le \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|} \le \frac{\max_{H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'} \deg_B(H')}{\min_{H \in {\mathcal{R}}} \deg_B(H)}.
nodes.label: eq_countingedges

nodes.name: Backward switching
nodes.statement: The reverse operation mapping $H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'$ to its neighbors in graph $B$, is called \emph{a backward switching}.

nodes.name: Family R_G and K = K_{n1,n2}
nodes.statement: For a fixed graph $G \subseteq K$ (possibly empty), where $K := K_{n_1,n_2}$, the families ${\mathcal{R}}, {\mathcal{R}}'$ will be subsets of \begin{equation} {\mathcal{R}}_G := \{ H \in {\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p) : G \subseteq H \}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Family R_G of biregular graphs containing G
nodes.statement: {\mathcal{R}}_G := \{ H \in {\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p) : G \subseteq H \}.
nodes.label: eq_rcG

nodes.name: Blue-red coloring induced by H
nodes.statement: Every $H \in {\mathcal{R}}_G$ will be interpreted as a blue-red coloring of the edges of $K\setminus G$: those in $H\setminus G$ will be colored \emph{blue} and those in $K \setminus H$ --- \emph{red}.

nodes.name: Color switching on a balanced edge set preserves biregularity
nodes.statement: Given $H\in{\mathcal{R}}$, consider a subset $S$ of the edges of $K\setminus G$ in which for every vertex $v \in V_1 \cup V_2$ the blue degree equals the red degree, i.e., $\deg_{(H\setminus G)\cap S}(v)=\deg_{(K\setminus H)\cap S}(v)$. Then switching the colors within $S$ produces another graph $H' \in {\mathcal{R}}_G$. Formally, $E(H')$ is the symmetric difference $E(H) \triangle S$.
nodes.statement_short: Switching colors on an edge set with equal blue and red degree at every vertex yields another graph of R_G.
assumptions: for every vertex $v \in V_1 \cup V_2$ the blue degree equals the red degree
conclusions: switching the colors within $S$ produces another graph $H' \in {\mathcal{R}}_G$

nodes.name: Alternating cycle (in K minus G)
nodes.statement: A cycle in $K\setminus G$ is \emph{alternating} if it is a union of a blue matching and a red matching.
differentia: union of a blue matching and a red matching

nodes.name: Families R_{G,e} and R_{G,not e}
nodes.statement: Given $e \in K\setminus G$, set \begin{equation} {\mathcal{R}}_{G,e} := \left\{ H \in {\mathcal{R}}_G : e \in H \right\}\qquad\text{and }\qquad {\mathcal{R}}_{G,\neg e} := \left\{ H \in {\mathcal{R}}_G : e \not\in H \right\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Families R_{G,e} and R_{G,not e}
nodes.statement: {\mathcal{R}}_{G,e} := \left\{ H \in {\mathcal{R}}_G : e \in H \right\}\qquad\text{and }\qquad {\mathcal{R}}_{G,\neg e} := \left\{ H \in {\mathcal{R}}_G : e \not\in H \right\}.
nodes.label: eq_rcGe

nodes.name: Switching ratio via short alternating cycles
nodes.statement_short: If e lies in an alternating cycle of length <= 2D for every H in R_G, then |R_{G,not e}|/|R_{G,e}| is between 1/(N^D-1) and N^D-1.
assumptions: Let a graph $G\subseteq K$ be such that ${\mathcal{R}}_G\neq\emptyset$ and let $e\in K\setminus G$.
Assume that for some number $D > 0$ and every $H\in {\mathcal{R}}_{G}$ the edge $e$ is contained in an alternating cycle of length at most $2D$.
nodes.label: prop_switch

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement:
Let $B = B({\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}, {\mathcal{R}}_{G,
eg e})$ be the switching graph corresponding to the following forward switching: choose an alternating cycle $S$ of length at most $2D$ containing $e$ and switch the colors of edges within $S$. Note that the backward switching does precisely the same. Note that by the assumption, the minimum degree $\delta(B)$ is at least $1$. Since ${\mathcal{R}}_G={\mathcal{R}}_{G, e}\cup{\mathcal{R}}_{G, 
eg e} 
eq \emptyset$, one of the classes ${\mathcal{R}}_{G, e}$ and ${\mathcal{R}}_{G, 
eg e}$ is non-empty and, in view of $\delta(B) \ge 1$, the other one is non-empty as well. For $\ell = 2, \dots, D$, the number of cycles of length $2\ell$ containing $e$ is, crudely, at most $n_1^{\ell - 1} n_2^{\ell - 1} = N^{\ell - 1}$, hence the maximum degree is \[ \Delta(B)\le N + N^2 + \cdots + N^{D - 1} \le N^D - 1. \] Thus, by~\eqref{eq_countingedges}, we obtain the claimed bounds.
nodes.statement_short: Switch along a short alternating cycle through e; bound min and max degree of the switching graph and use double counting.

nodes.name: Define the cycle switching
nodes.statement: Let $B = B({\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}, {\mathcal{R}}_{G,\neg e})$ be the switching graph corresponding to the following forward switching: choose an alternating cycle $S$ of length at most $2D$ containing $e$ and switch the colors of edges within $S$. Note that the backward switching does precisely the same.
nodes.statement_short: Switch colors along an alternating cycle of length <= 2D through e.

nodes.name: Minimum degree of B
nodes.statement: Note that by the assumption, the minimum degree $\delta(B)$ is at least $1$.
nodes.statement_short: By assumption delta(B) >= 1.

nodes.name: Both classes non-empty
nodes.statement:
Since ${\mathcal{R}}_G={\mathcal{R}}_{G, e}\cup{\mathcal{R}}_{G, 
eg e} 
eq \emptyset$, one of the classes ${\mathcal{R}}_{G, e}$ and ${\mathcal{R}}_{G, 
eg e}$ is non-empty and, in view of $\delta(B) \ge 1$, the other one is non-empty as well.
nodes.statement_short: R_G non-empty and delta(B)>=1 make both classes non-empty.

nodes.name: Maximum degree of B
nodes.statement: For $\ell = 2, \dots, D$, the number of cycles of length $2\ell$ containing $e$ is, crudely, at most $n_1^{\ell - 1} n_2^{\ell - 1} = N^{\ell - 1}$, hence the maximum degree is \[ \Delta(B)\le N + N^2 + \cdots + N^{D - 1} \le N^D - 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Count cycles through e to get Delta(B) <= N^D - 1.

nodes.name: Conclude via double counting
nodes.statement: Thus, by~\eqref{eq_countingedges}, we obtain the claimed bounds.
nodes.statement_short: Apply eq_countingedges.

nodes.name: Chernoff bounds
nodes.statement: For a sum $X $ of independent Bernoulli (not necessarily identically distributed) random variables, writing $\mu = \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} X$, we have (see Theorem 2.8, (2.5), (2.6), and~(2.11) in~\cite{JLR} that \begin{equation} \prob{X \ge \mu + t} \le \exp \left\{ - \frac{t^2}{2\left( \mu + t/3 \right)} \right\}, \qquad t \ge 0, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \prob{X \le \mu - t} \le \exp \left\{ - \frac{t^2}{2\mu} \right\}, \qquad t \ge 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Upper and lower Chernoff tail bounds for sums of independent Bernoulli variables.
assumptions: For a sum $X $ of independent Bernoulli (not necessarily identically distributed) random variables, writing $\mu = \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} X$

nodes.name: Chernoff upper tail bound
nodes.statement: \prob{X \ge \mu + t} \le \exp \left\{ - \frac{t^2}{2\left( \mu + t/3 \right)} \right\}, \qquad t \ge 0,
nodes.label: eq_hypergeomUpTailExp

nodes.name: Chernoff lower tail bound
nodes.statement: \prob{X \le \mu - t} \le \exp \left\{ - \frac{t^2}{2\mu} \right\}, \qquad t \ge 0.
nodes.label: eq_hypergeomLowTailExp

nodes.name: Hypergeometric distribution Hyp(g,a,r)
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a set of size $|\Gamma|=g$ and let $A \subseteq \Gamma$, $|A|=a \ge1$. For an integer $r \in [0,g]$, choose uniformly at random a subset $R \subseteq \Gamma$ of size $|R|=r$. The random variable $Y = |A \cap R|$ has then the \emph{hypergeometric} distribution $\operatorname{Hyp}(g, a, r)$ with expectation $\mu := \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} Y = ar/g$.

nodes.name: Chernoff bounds for hypergeometric variables
nodes.statement: By Theorem 2.10 in~\cite{JLR}, inequalities~\eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} and~\eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp} hold for $Y$, too.

nodes.name: Chernoff bounds for Poisson variables
nodes.statement: Moreover, by Remark 2.6 in~\cite{JLR}, inequalities~\eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} and~\eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp} also hold for a random variable $Z$ which has Poisson distribution $\operatorname{Po}(\mu)$ with expectation $\mu$.

nodes.name: Poisson mode probability lower bound
nodes.statement: For $k\ge0$, set $q_k=\prob{Z=k}$. Then $q_k/q_{k-1}=\mu/k$, and hence $k = \lfloor\mu\rfloor$ maximizes $q_k$ (we say that such $k$ is a \emph{mode} of $Z$). Since $\operatorname {Var} Z = \mu$, by Chebyshev's inequality, $\prob{|Z-\mu|<\sqrt{2\mu}}\ge1/2$. Moreover, the interval $(\mu - \sqrt{2 \mu}, \mu + \sqrt{2 \mu})$ contains at most $\lceil \sqrt{8\mu}\:\rceil$ integers, hence it follows that \begin{equation} q_{\lfloor \mu \rfloor} \ge \frac{1/2}{\lceil \sqrt{8\mu}\: \rceil}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Poisson mode floor(mu) has probability at least (1/2)/ceil(sqrt(8 mu)).

nodes.name: Lower bound on Poisson mode probability
nodes.statement: q_{\lfloor \mu \rfloor} \ge \frac{1/2}{\lceil \sqrt{8\mu}\: \rceil}.
nodes.label: eq_largestatom

nodes.name: Class R(d_1,d_2) of bipartite graphs with given degrees
nodes.statement: Given two vectors $\mathbf{d}_1 = (d_{1,v}, v \in V_1)$ and $\mathbf{d}_2 = (d_{2,v}, v \in V_2)$ of positive integers such that $\sum_{v \in V_1} d_{1, v} = \sum_{v \in V_2} d_{2,v}$, let ${\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)$ be the class of bipartite graphs on $(V_1, V_2)$ with vertex degrees $\deg(v) = d_{i,v}, v \in V_i, i = 1,2$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Asymptotic enumeration of dense bipartite graphs

nodes.name: Average degrees, variances D_i and density p
nodes.statement: Let $|V_i| = n_i$ and write $\bar d_i = {n_i}^{-1}\sum_{v \in V_i} d_{i,v}$, $D_i = \sum_{v \in V_i} (d_{i,v} - \bar d_i)^2$, $p = \bar d_1/n_2 = \bar d_2/n_1$, and $q = 1 - p$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Asymptotic enumeration of dense bipartite graphs

nodes.name: Canfield-Greenhill-McKay asymptotic enumeration of dense bipartite graphs
nodes.statement: Given any positive constants $a, b, C$ such that $a+b < 1/2$, there exists a constant $\epsilon > 0$ so that the following holds. Consider the set of degree sequences $\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2$ satisfying \begin{romenumerate} \item $\max_{v \in V_1}|d_{1,v} - \bar d_1| \le Cn_2^{1/2 + \epsilon}$, $\max_{v \in V_2} |d_{2,v} - \bar d_2| \le Cn_1^{1/2 + \epsilon}$ \item $\max \{n_1, n_2\} \le C(pq)^2(\min \left\{ n_1, n_2 \right\})^{1 + \epsilon}$ \item $ \frac{(1 - 2p)^2}{4pq} \left( 1 + \frac{5n_1}{6n_2} + \frac{5n_2}{6n_1} \right) \le a \log \max \left\{ n_1, n_2 \right\}$. \end{romenumerate} If $\min\{n_1, n_2\} \to \infty$, then uniformly for all such $\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2$ \begin{multline} |{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)| = \binom{n_1n_2}{p n_1n_2}^{-1} \prod_{v \in V_1}\binom {n_2}{d_{1,v}} \prod_{v \in V_2}\binom {n_1}{d_{2,v}} \times \\ \times \exp \left[ -\frac{1}{2}\left( 1- \frac{D_1}{pqn_1n_2} \right)\left(1- \frac{D_2}{pqn_1n_2} \right) + O\left((\max\left\{ n_1,n_2 \right\})^{-b}\right) \right], \end{multline} where the constants implicit in the error term may depend on $a,b,C$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Asymptotic enumeration of dense bipartite graphs
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic formula for the number of bipartite graphs with given near-regular degree sequences in the dense regime.
assumptions: Given any positive constants $a, b, C$ such that $a+b < 1/2$
If $\min\{n_1, n_2\} \to \infty$
nodes.label: thm_enum

nodes.name: Canfield-Greenhill-McKay enumeration formula
nodes.statement: |{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)| = \binom{n_1n_2}{p n_1n_2}^{-1} \prod_{v \in V_1}\binom {n_2}{d_{1,v}} \prod_{v \in V_2}\binom {n_1}{d_{2,v}} \times \\ \times \exp \left[ -\frac{1}{2}\left( 1- \frac{D_1}{pqn_1n_2} \right)\left(1- \frac{D_2}{pqn_1n_2} \right) + O\left((\max\left\{ n_1,n_2 \right\})^{-b}\right) \right],
nodes.section: 2.4 Asymptotic enumeration of dense bipartite graphs
nodes.label: eq_enum

nodes.name: Reformulation of the CGM conditions
nodes.statement: Note that condition~\ref{thm_enum_balance} of Theorem~\ref{thm_enum} implies the corresponding condition in~\cite{CGM} after adjusting~$\epsilon$. Also, the uniformity of the bound is not explicitly stated in~\cite{CGM}, but, given $n_1, n_2$, one should take $\mathbf{d}_1, \mathbf{d}_2$ with the worst error and apply the result in~\cite{CGM}.
nodes.section: 2.4 Asymptotic enumeration of dense bipartite graphs

nodes.name: Erdos-Renyi random graph process G(t)
nodes.statement: Consider a sequence of graphs $\mathbb G(t) \subseteq K$ for $t = 0, \dots , N$, where $\mathbb G(0)$ is empty and, for $t < N$, $\mathbb G(t + 1)$ is obtained from $\mathbb G(t)$ by adding an edge $\varepsilon_{t + 1}$ chosen from $K \setminus \mathbb G(t)$ uniformly at random, that is, for every graph $G \subseteq K$ of size $t$ and every edge $e \in K \setminus G$ \begin{equation} \Pc{\varepsilon_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb G(t) = G} = \frac{1}{N - t}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Uniform edge addition probability in G(t)
nodes.statement: \Pc{\varepsilon_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb G(t) = G} = \frac{1}{N - t}.
nodes.label: eq_PG

nodes.name: Random ordering of edges of R(n1,n2,p)
nodes.statement: Recalling that a $p$-biregular graph has $M = pN$ edges, let \begin{equation*} (\eta_1, \dots, \eta_M) \end{equation*} be a uniformly random ordering of the edges of $\mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$.

nodes.name: Random biregular graph process R(t)
nodes.statement: By taking the initial segments, we obtain a sequence of random graphs \begin{equation*} \mathbb R(t) = \{\eta_1, \dots, \eta_t\}, \qquad t = 0, \dots, M. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Shorthand R = R(M)
nodes.statement: For convenience, we shorten \[ \mathbb R:= \mathbb R(M) = \mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)\;. \]

nodes.name: R(t) given R=H is a uniform t-subset
nodes.statement: Let us mention here that for a fixed $H \in {\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)$, conditioning on $\mathbb R = H$, the edge set of the random subgraph $\mathbb R(t)$ is a uniformly random $t$-element subset of the edge set of~$H$.
conclusions: the edge set of the random subgraph  $\mathbb R(t)$ is a uniformly random $t$-element subset of the edge set of~$H$

nodes.name: Admissible graph
nodes.statement: We say that a graph $G$ with $t$ edges is \emph{admissible}, if the family ${\mathcal{R}}_G$ (see definition~\eqref{eq_rcG}) is nonempty, or, equivalently, \begin{equation*} \prob{\mathbb R(t) = G} > 0. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Conditional next-edge probability p_{t+1}(e,G)
nodes.statement: For an admissible graph $G$ with $t$ edges and any edge $ e \in K \setminus G$, let \begin{equation} p_{t+1}(e,G) := \Pc{\eta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R(t) = G}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Conditional next-edge probability p_{t+1}(e,G)
nodes.statement: p_{t+1}(e,G) := \Pc{\eta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R(t) = G}.
nodes.label: eq_pt

nodes.name: Description of the conditional space for p_{t+1}
nodes.statement: The conditional space underlying~\eqref{eq_pt} can be described as first extending $G$ uniformly at random to an element of ${\mathcal{R}}_G$ and then randomly permuting the new $M-t$ edges.

nodes.name: Event A(t,chi)
nodes.statement: Given a real number $\chi \ge 0$ and $t \in \{0, \dots, M - 1\}$, we define an $\mathbb R(t)$-measurable event \begin{equation*} {\mathcal{A}}(t,\chi) := \left\{ p_{t+1}(e,\mathbb R(t)) \ge \frac{1 - \chi}{N - t} \text{ for every } e \in K \setminus \mathbb R(t) \right\}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Event A
nodes.statement: Postponing the choice of $\gamma_t$ and $t_0$, we define an event \begin{equation} {\mathcal{A}} := \bigcap_{t = 0}^{ t_0 - 1}{\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Event A (almost uniform up to t_0)
nodes.statement: {\mathcal{A}} := \bigcap_{t = 0}^{ t_0 - 1}{\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t).
nodes.label: eq_ac

nodes.name: Time parameter tau
nodes.statement: For this, we define by \begin{equation} \tau = \tau(t) := 1 - \frac{t}{M} \in [0,1]\qquad\text{and so}\qquad t = (1 - \tau)M. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Time parametrization tau
nodes.statement: \tau = \tau(t) := 1 - \frac{t}{M} \in [0,1]\qquad\text{and so}\qquad t = (1 - \tau)M.
nodes.label: eq_tau

nodes.name: Final time parameter tau_0
nodes.statement: Given a constant $C > 0$ and, we define (recalling the notation in~\eqref{eq_not}) the ``final'' value $\tau_0$ of~$\tau$~as \begin{equation} \tau_0 := \begin{cases} \frac{3 \cdot 3240^2(C + 4)\log N}{p \hat n}, \quad & p \le 0.49, \\ 700(3(C + 4))^{1/4} \left( q^{3/2}\mathbb I + \left(\frac{\log N}{\hat n}\right)^{1/4}\right), \quad & p > 0.49. \end{cases} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Final value tau_0
nodes.statement: \tau_0 := \begin{cases} \frac{3 \cdot 3240^2(C + 4)\log N}{p \hat n}, \quad & p \le 0.49, \\ 700(3(C + 4))^{1/4} \left( q^{3/2}\mathbb I + \left(\frac{\log N}{\hat n}\right)^{1/4}\right), \quad & p > 0.49. \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq_tauzero

nodes.name: Assumptions on p (eq_phat_lower, eq_hatpI_ubound, eq_ef_qlbound)
nodes.statement: Consider the following assumptions on $p$ (which we will later show to follow from the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}): \begin{equation} \hat p \ge \frac{3 \cdot 3240^2(C+4)\log N}{\hat n}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \hat p \cdot \mathbb I \le \frac{49}{51}\cdot\frac1{340^2 (C + 4)^{1/6}}, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} q \ge 680\left( \frac{3(C+4)\log N}{\hat{n}}\right)^{1/4}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound on p-hat, upper bound on p-hat*I, lower bound on q.

nodes.name: Assumption: lower bound on p-hat
nodes.statement: \hat p \ge \frac{3 \cdot 3240^2(C+4)\log N}{\hat n},
nodes.label: eq_phat_lower

nodes.name: Assumption: upper bound on p-hat * I
nodes.statement: \hat p \cdot \mathbb I \le \frac{49}{51}\cdot\frac1{340^2 (C + 4)^{1/6}},
nodes.label: eq_hatpI_ubound

nodes.name: Assumption: lower bound on q
nodes.statement: q \ge 680\left( \frac{3(C+4)\log N}{\hat{n}}\right)^{1/4}.
nodes.label: eq_ef_qlbound

nodes.name: tau_0 <= 1 and definition of t_0
nodes.statement: At the end of this subsection we show that these three assumptions imply \begin{equation} \tau_0 \le 1, \end{equation} so that \begin{equation*} t_0 := \lfloor (1 - \tau_0)M \rfloor \end{equation*} is a non-negative integer.
nodes.statement_short: The three assumptions give tau_0 <= 1, so t_0 = floor((1-tau_0)M) is a non-negative integer.
assumptions: these three assumptions

nodes.name: tau_0 <= 1
nodes.statement: \tau_0 \le 1,
nodes.label: eq_tau_less

nodes.name: Coupling parameters gamma_t
nodes.statement: Further, for $t = 0, \dots, M - 1$, define \begin{equation} \gamma_t := 1080 \hat p^2 \mathbb I + \begin{cases} 3240 \sqrt{\frac{2(C + 3)\log N}{\tau p \hat n}}, \quad & p \le 0.49, \\ 25000 \sqrt{\frac{(C + 3)\log N}{ \tau^2q^2 \hat n}} , \quad & p > 0.49. \end{cases} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Coupling parameter gamma_t
nodes.statement: \gamma_t := 1080 \hat p^2 \mathbb I + \begin{cases} 3240 \sqrt{\frac{2(C + 3)\log N}{\tau p \hat n}}, \quad & p \le 0.49, \\ 25000 \sqrt{\frac{(C + 3)\log N}{ \tau^2q^2 \hat n}} , \quad & p > 0.49. \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq_gamma_t

nodes.name: Crucial lemma: the process R(t) stays almost uniform
nodes.statement: For every constant $C > 0$, if assumptions~\eqref{eq_phat_lower},~\eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound}, and~\eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} hold, then \begin{equation} \prob{{\mathcal{A}}} = 1- O(N^{-C}), \end{equation} where the constant implicit in the $O$-term in~\eqref{eq_largeprob} may also depend on $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Under the assumptions on p, a.a.s. (prob. 1-O(N^{-C})) every next-edge probability is at least (1-gamma_t)/(N-t) for all t<t_0.
assumptions: For every constant $C > 0$, if assumptions~\eqref{eq_phat_lower},~\eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound}, and~\eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} hold
nodes.label: lem_Stanislaw

nodes.name: Event A holds with probability 1-O(N^{-C})
nodes.statement: \prob{{\mathcal{A}}} = 1- O(N^{-C}),
nodes.label: eq_largeprob

nodes.name: Proof that tau_0 <= 1
nodes.statement: It remains to show~\eqref{eq_tau_less}. When $p \le 0.49$, inequality~\eqref{eq_tau_less} is equivalent to~\eqref{eq_phat_lower}. For $p > 0.49$, we have $q \le 51\hat p/49$, which together with assumptions~\eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} and~\eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} implies that \[ \tau_0 \le 700 \left( 3(C+4) \right)^{1/4} \left( \frac{51}{49}\hat p \cdot \mathbb I \right)^{3/2} + 700 \cdot \frac{q}{680} \le \frac{700 \cdot 3^{1/4}}{340^3} + \frac{700 \cdot 0.51}{680} < 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Case p<=0.49 is the assumption itself; for p>0.49 bound tau_0 using q <= 51 p-hat/49 and the assumptions.

nodes.name: Case p <= 0.49
nodes.statement: It remains to show~\eqref{eq_tau_less}. When $p \le 0.49$, inequality~\eqref{eq_tau_less} is equivalent to~\eqref{eq_phat_lower}.
nodes.statement_short: For p <= 0.49 the claim is eq_phat_lower.

nodes.name: Case p > 0.49
nodes.statement: For $p > 0.49$, we have $q \le 51\hat p/49$, which together with assumptions~\eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} and~\eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} implies that \[ \tau_0 \le 700 \left( 3(C+4) \right)^{1/4} \left( \frac{51}{49}\hat p \cdot \mathbb I \right)^{3/2} + 700 \cdot \frac{q}{680} \le \frac{700 \cdot 3^{1/4}}{340^3} + \frac{700 \cdot 0.51}{680} < 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound tau_0 by the assumptions on p-hat*I and q.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: From Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw} we are going to deduce Theorem~\ref{thm_embed} using a coupling argument similar to the one which was employed by Dudek, Frieze, Ruci\'nski and \v{S}ileikis~\cite{DFRSc}, but with an extra tweak (inspired by Kim and Vu~\cite{KV04}) of letting the probabilities~$\gamma_t$ of Bernoulli random variables depend on $t$, which reduces the error $\gamma$ in~\eqref{eq_gamma}. It is easy to check that the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw} follow from the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}. Indeed,~\eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} coincides with assumption~\eqref{eq:thm_embed_q}, while~\eqref{eq_phat_lower} and~\eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} follow from the assumption $\gamma \le 1$ (see~\eqref{eq_gamma}) for sufficiently large $C^*$. \medskip Our aim is to couple $(\mathbb G(t))_t$ and $(\mathbb R(t))_t$ on the event ${\mathcal{A}}$ defined in~\eqref{eq_ac}. For this we will define a graph process $\mathbb R'(t) := \{\eta'_1, \dots, \eta'_t\}, t = 0, \dots, t_0$ so that for every admissible graph~$G$ with $t \in [0, M -1]$ edges and every $e \in K \setminus G$ \begin{equation} \Pc{\eta'_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R'(t) = G} = p_{t+1}(e, G), \end{equation} where $p_{t+1}(e, G)$ was defined in~\eqref{eq_pt}. Note that $\mathbb R'(0)$ is an empty graph. Since the distribution of the process $(\mathbb R(t))_t$ is determined by the conditional probabilities~\eqref{eq_pt}, in view of~\eqref{eq_etaprime}, the distribution of $\mathbb R'(t_0)$ is the same as that of $\mathbb R(t_0)$ and therefore we will identify $\mathbb R'(t_0)$ with $\mathbb R(t_0)$. As the second step, we will show that a.a.s.\ $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ can be sampled from $\mathbb R'(t_0) = \mathbb R(t_0)$. Proceeding with the definition, set $\mathbb R'(0)$ to be the empty graph and define graphs $\mathbb R'(t)$, $t = 1, \dots, t_0$, inductively, as follows. Hence, let us further fix $t \in [0, t_0-1]$ and suppose that \[ \mathbb R'(t)=R_t\quad\mbox{and}\quad \mathbb G(t)=G_t \] have been already chosen. Our immediate goal is to select a random pair of edges $\varepsilon_{t+1}$ and $\eta_{t+1}'$, according to, resp.,~\eqref{eq_PG} and~\eqref{eq_etaprime}, in such a way that the event $\varepsilon_{t+1}\in \mathbb R'(t+1)$ is quite likely. To this end, draw $\varepsilon_{t + 1}$ uniformly at random from $K \setminus G_t$ and, independently, generate a Bernoulli random variable $\xi_{t+1}$ with the probability of success $1 - \gamma_t$ (which is in $[0,1]$ by~\eqref{eq_gammat_less1}). If event ${\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t)$ has occurred, that is, if \begin{equation} p_{t+1}(e, R_t) \ge \frac{1 - \gamma_t}{N - t} \quad \text{ for every } \quad e \in K \setminus R_t, \end{equation} then draw a random edge $\zeta_{t+1} \in K \setminus R_t$ according to the distribution \begin{equation*} \Pc{\zeta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R'(t) = R_t} := \frac{p_{t+1}(e, R_t) - (1 - \gamma_t)/(N - t) }{\gamma_t} \ge 0, \end{equation*} where the inequality holds by~\eqref{eq_coupling}. Observe also that \begin{equation*} \sum_{e\in K \setminus R_t}\Pc{\zeta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R'(t) = R_t} = 1, \end{equation*} so $\zeta_{t+1}$ has a properly defined distribution. Finally, fix an arbitrary bijection \[ f_{R_t, G_t} : R_t \setminus G_t \to G_t \setminus R_t \] between the sets of edges and define \begin{equation*} \eta'_{t+1} = \begin{cases} \varepsilon_{t+1}, &\text{ if } \xi_{t + 1} = 1, \varepsilon_{t+1} \in K \setminus R_t,\\ f_{R_t, G_t}(\varepsilon_{t+1}), &\text{ if } \xi_{t + 1} = 1, \varepsilon_{t+1} \in R_t,\\ \zeta_{t+1}, &\text{ if } \xi_{t + 1} = 0. \\ \end{cases} \end{equation*} On the other hand, if event ${\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t)$ has failed, then $\eta'_{t+1}$ is sampled directly (without defining $\zeta_{t+1}$) according to the distribution~\eqref{eq_etaprime}. With this definition of $(\mathbb R'(t))_{t= 0}^{t_0}$, it is easy to check that for $\eta'_{t+1}$ defined above,~\eqref{eq_etaprime} indeed holds, so from now on we drop the prime $'$ and identify $\mathbb R'(t)$ with $\mathbb R(t)$, which is a subset of $\mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$. Most importantly, we conclude that, for $t = 0, \cdots, t_0 - 1$ \begin{equation} {\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t) \cap \{\xi_{t+1} = 1\} \quad \implies \quad \varepsilon_{t+1} \in \mathbb R(t+1). \end{equation} In view of this, define \begin{equation*} S := \left\{ t \in [t_0] : \xi_t = 1 \right\} \end{equation*} and recall that $m=\lceil (1-\gamma)M\rceil$. If $|S| \ge m$, define $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ as, say, the edges indexed by the smallest $m$ elements of $S$ (note that since the vectors $(\xi_i)$ and $(\varepsilon_i)$ are independent, after conditioning on $S$, these $m$ edges are uniformly distributed), and if $|S| < m$, then define $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ as, say, the graph with edges $\{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_m\}$. Recalling the definition~\eqref{eq_ac} of the event ${\mathcal{A}}$, by~\eqref{eq_implies} we observe that ${\mathcal{A}}$ implies the inclusion $\left\{ \varepsilon_t : t \in S \right\} \subseteq \mathbb R(t_0) \subset \mathbb R(M) = \mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$. On the other hand $|S| \ge m$ implies $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m) \subseteq \left\{ \varepsilon_t : t \in S \right\}$, so \begin{equation*} \prob{\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m) \subseteq \mathbb R} \ge \prob{\{|S| \ge m\}\cap {\mathcal{A}} }. \end{equation*} Since, by Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}, event ${\mathcal{A}}$ holds with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$, to complete the proof of~\eqref{eq_lower_embed} it suffices to show that also \begin{equation*} \prob{|S| \ge m} = 1 - O(N^{-C}) . \end{equation*} For this we need the following claim whose technical proof is deferred to Section~\ref{sec_technical}. \begin{claim} We have \begin{equation} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} |S| \ge t_0 - \theta M, \end{equation} where \begin{equation*} \theta := 1080 \hat p^2 \mathbb I + \begin{cases} 6480\sqrt{\frac{2(C + 3)\log N}{p\hat n}}, &\quad p \le 0.49, \\ 6250\sqrt{\frac{(C + 3)\log N}{q^2\hat n } }\log \frac{\hat n}{\log N}, &\quad p > 0.49, \end{cases} \end{equation*} and, with $\gamma$ as in~\eqref{eq_gamma}, \begin{equation} \gamma \ge \tau_0 + \theta + 2/M + \sqrt{\frac{2C \log N}{M}}. \end{equation} \end{claim} \medskip Recalling that $t_0 = \lfloor (1 - \tau_0)M \rfloor$ and $m = \lceil(1-\gamma)M\rceil$, we have \begin{equation} \begin{split} t_0 - \theta M - m &\ge (1-\tau_0)M - 1 - \theta M - (1-\gamma)M - 1 \\ &= (\gamma - \tau_0 - \theta)M - 2 \By{\eqref{eq_thetaM}}{\ge} \sqrt{2C M \log N}. \end{split} \end{equation} Since $|S|$ is a sum of independent Bernoulli random variables, \begin{align*} \prob{|S| < m} &= \prob{|S| < \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|S|- (\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|S| - m) } \By{\eqref{eq_theta_p}}{\le} \prob{|S| < \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|S| -(t_0 - \theta M - m)} \\ \justify{\eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}, $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}} |S| \le M$} &\By{}{\le} \exp \left( -\frac{(t_0 - \theta M - m)^2}{2M} \right) \By{\eqref{eq_tzero_theta_Mm}}{\le} \exp \left( - C \log N \right) = N^{-C}, \end{align*} which as mentioned above, implies~\eqref{eq_lower_embed}. \medskip Finally, we prove~\eqref{eq:embed_Gnp} by coupling $\mathbb G(n_1, n_2, p')$ with $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2, m)$ so that the former is a subset of the latter with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$. Denote by $X := e(\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p'))$ the number of edges of $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2, p')$. Whenever $X \le m$, choose $X$ edges of $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ at random and declare them to be a copy of $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p')$. Otherwise sample $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p')$ independently from $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$. Hence it remains to show that $\prob{X > m} = O(N^{-C})$. Recalling that $m = \ceil{(1-\gamma)}pN$ and $p' = (1 - 2\gamma)p$, we have $m/N \ge (1 - \gamma)p = p' + \gamma p$. Since $X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(N,p')$, Chernoff's bound~\eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} implies that \begin{equation} \prob{X > m} \le \prob{X > p'N + \gamma p N} \le \exp\left\{ -\frac{(\gamma pN)^2}{2(p'N + \gamma pN/3)} \right\} \le e^{-\gamma^2pN/2}. \end{equation} Choosing $C^*$ sufficiently large, the definition~\eqref{eq_gamma} implies $\gamma \ge \sqrt{\frac{2C\log N}{p N}}$ with a lot of room (to see this easier in the case $p > 0.49$, note that \eqref{eq:thm_embed_q} implies $\log(\hat n/\log N) \ge 1$, say). So~\eqref{eq:Xmorem} implies $\prob{X > m} \le N^{-C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Coupling: build R(t) step by step so that a Bernoulli(1-gamma_t) success forces the uniform edge into R(t+1) on the event A. Chernoff then shows |S| >= m w.h.p.

nodes.name: Strategy: coupling
nodes.statement: From Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw} we are going to deduce Theorem~\ref{thm_embed} using a coupling argument similar to the one which was employed by Dudek, Frieze, Ruci\'nski and \v{S}ileikis~\cite{DFRSc}, but with an extra tweak (inspired by Kim and Vu~\cite{KV04}) of letting the probabilities~$\gamma_t$ of Bernoulli random variables depend on $t$, which reduces the error $\gamma$ in~\eqref{eq_gamma}.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce Theorem 2 from Lemma 6 via a coupling with t-dependent gamma_t.

nodes.name: Check Lemma 6 applies
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw} follow from the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}. Indeed,~\eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} coincides with assumption~\eqref{eq:thm_embed_q}, while~\eqref{eq_phat_lower} and~\eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} follow from the assumption $\gamma \le 1$ (see~\eqref{eq_gamma}) for sufficiently large $C^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2's assumptions imply those of Lemma 6.

nodes.name: Plan of the coupling
nodes.statement: Our aim is to couple $(\mathbb G(t))_t$ and $(\mathbb R(t))_t$ on the event ${\mathcal{A}}$ defined in~\eqref{eq_ac}. For this we will define a graph process $\mathbb R'(t) := \{\eta'_1, \dots, \eta'_t\}, t = 0, \dots, t_0$ so that for every admissible graph~$G$ with $t \in [0, M -1]$ edges and every $e \in K \setminus G$ \begin{equation} \Pc{\eta'_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R'(t) = G} = p_{t+1}(e, G), \end{equation} where $p_{t+1}(e, G)$ was defined in~\eqref{eq_pt}. Note that $\mathbb R'(0)$ is an empty graph. Since the distribution of the process $(\mathbb R(t))_t$ is determined by the conditional probabilities~\eqref{eq_pt}, in view of~\eqref{eq_etaprime}, the distribution of $\mathbb R'(t_0)$ is the same as that of $\mathbb R(t_0)$ and therefore we will identify $\mathbb R'(t_0)$ with $\mathbb R(t_0)$. As the second step, we will show that a.a.s.\ $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ can be sampled from $\mathbb R'(t_0) = \mathbb R(t_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define a process R'(t) with the same transition probabilities as R(t).

nodes.name: Transition probabilities of R'(t)
nodes.statement: \Pc{\eta'_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R'(t) = G} = p_{t+1}(e, G),
nodes.label: eq_etaprime

nodes.name: Construct the coupled step
nodes.statement: Proceeding with the definition, set $\mathbb R'(0)$ to be the empty graph and define graphs $\mathbb R'(t)$, $t = 1, \dots, t_0$, inductively, as follows. Hence, let us further fix $t \in [0, t_0-1]$ and suppose that \[ \mathbb R'(t)=R_t\quad\mbox{and}\quad \mathbb G(t)=G_t \] have been already chosen. Our immediate goal is to select a random pair of edges $\varepsilon_{t+1}$ and $\eta_{t+1}'$, according to, resp.,~\eqref{eq_PG} and~\eqref{eq_etaprime}, in such a way that the event $\varepsilon_{t+1}\in \mathbb R'(t+1)$ is quite likely. To this end, draw $\varepsilon_{t + 1}$ uniformly at random from $K \setminus G_t$ and, independently, generate a Bernoulli random variable $\xi_{t+1}$ with the probability of success $1 - \gamma_t$ (which is in $[0,1]$ by~\eqref{eq_gammat_less1}). If event ${\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t)$ has occurred, that is, if \begin{equation} p_{t+1}(e, R_t) \ge \frac{1 - \gamma_t}{N - t} \quad \text{ for every } \quad e \in K \setminus R_t, \end{equation} then draw a random edge $\zeta_{t+1} \in K \setminus R_t$ according to the distribution \begin{equation*} \Pc{\zeta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R'(t) = R_t} := \frac{p_{t+1}(e, R_t) - (1 - \gamma_t)/(N - t) }{\gamma_t} \ge 0, \end{equation*} where the inequality holds by~\eqref{eq_coupling}. Observe also that \begin{equation*} \sum_{e\in K \setminus R_t}\Pc{\zeta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R'(t) = R_t} = 1, \end{equation*} so $\zeta_{t+1}$ has a properly defined distribution. Finally, fix an arbitrary bijection \[ f_{R_t, G_t} : R_t \setminus G_t \to G_t \setminus R_t \] between the sets of edges and define \begin{equation*} \eta'_{t+1} = \begin{cases} \varepsilon_{t+1}, &\text{ if } \xi_{t + 1} = 1, \varepsilon_{t+1} \in K \setminus R_t,\\ f_{R_t, G_t}(\varepsilon_{t+1}), &\text{ if } \xi_{t + 1} = 1, \varepsilon_{t+1} \in R_t,\\ \zeta_{t+1}, &\text{ if } \xi_{t + 1} = 0. \\ \end{cases} \end{equation*} On the other hand, if event ${\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t)$ has failed, then $\eta'_{t+1}$ is sampled directly (without defining $\zeta_{t+1}$) according to the distribution~\eqref{eq_etaprime}.
nodes.statement_short: Draw eps_{t+1} uniformly and xi_{t+1} ~ Bernoulli(1-gamma_t); on A(t,gamma_t) choose eta'_{t+1} to contain eps_{t+1} when xi=1.

nodes.name: Event A(t,gamma_t) inequality
nodes.statement: p_{t+1}(e, R_t) \ge \frac{1 - \gamma_t}{N - t} \quad \text{ for every } \quad e \in K \setminus R_t,
nodes.label: eq_coupling

nodes.name: Identify R'(t) with R(t)
nodes.statement: With this definition of $(\mathbb R'(t))_{t= 0}^{t_0}$, it is easy to check that for $\eta'_{t+1}$ defined above,~\eqref{eq_etaprime} indeed holds, so from now on we drop the prime $'$ and identify $\mathbb R'(t)$ with $\mathbb R(t)$, which is a subset of $\mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$.
nodes.statement_short: The construction has the right law, so R'(t) = R(t).

nodes.name: Key implication
nodes.statement: Most importantly, we conclude that, for $t = 0, \cdots, t_0 - 1$ \begin{equation} {\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t) \cap \{\xi_{t+1} = 1\} \quad \implies \quad \varepsilon_{t+1} \in \mathbb R(t+1). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On A(t,gamma_t), xi_{t+1}=1 forces eps_{t+1} into R(t+1).

nodes.name: A(t,gamma_t) and xi=1 imply epsilon in R(t+1)
nodes.statement: {\mathcal{A}}(t, \gamma_t) \cap \{\xi_{t+1} = 1\} \quad \implies \quad \varepsilon_{t+1} \in \mathbb R(t+1).
nodes.label: eq_implies

nodes.name: Define S and G(n1,n2,m)
nodes.statement: In view of this, define \begin{equation*} S := \left\{ t \in [t_0] : \xi_t = 1 \right\} \end{equation*} and recall that $m=\lceil (1-\gamma)M\rceil$. If $|S| \ge m$, define $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ as, say, the edges indexed by the smallest $m$ elements of $S$ (note that since the vectors $(\xi_i)$ and $(\varepsilon_i)$ are independent, after conditioning on $S$, these $m$ edges are uniformly distributed), and if $|S| < m$, then define $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ as, say, the graph with edges $\{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_m\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Let S be the success times and take G(n1,n2,m) from the first m of them.

nodes.name: Reduce to |S| >= m and A
nodes.statement: Recalling the definition~\eqref{eq_ac} of the event ${\mathcal{A}}$, by~\eqref{eq_implies} we observe that ${\mathcal{A}}$ implies the inclusion $\left\{ \varepsilon_t : t \in S \right\} \subseteq \mathbb R(t_0) \subset \mathbb R(M) = \mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$. On the other hand $|S| \ge m$ implies $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m) \subseteq \left\{ \varepsilon_t : t \in S \right\}$, so \begin{equation*} \prob{\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m) \subseteq \mathbb R} \ge \prob{\{|S| \ge m\}\cap {\mathcal{A}} }. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: P(G subset R) >= P(|S|>=m and A).

nodes.name: Suffices: |S| >= m w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Since, by Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}, event ${\mathcal{A}}$ holds with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$, to complete the proof of~\eqref{eq_lower_embed} it suffices to show that also \begin{equation*} \prob{|S| \ge m} = 1 - O(N^{-C}) . \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 6 it suffices to show P(|S|>=m) = 1-O(N^{-C}).

nodes.name: Invoke Claim 7
nodes.statement: For this we need the following claim whose technical proof is deferred to Section~\ref{sec_technical}. \begin{claim} We have \begin{equation} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} |S| \ge t_0 - \theta M, \end{equation} where \begin{equation*} \theta := 1080 \hat p^2 \mathbb I + \begin{cases} 6480\sqrt{\frac{2(C + 3)\log N}{p\hat n}}, &\quad p \le 0.49, \\ 6250\sqrt{\frac{(C + 3)\log N}{q^2\hat n } }\log \frac{\hat n}{\log N}, &\quad p > 0.49, \end{cases} \end{equation*} and, with $\gamma$ as in~\eqref{eq_gamma}, \begin{equation} \gamma \ge \tau_0 + \theta + 2/M + \sqrt{\frac{2C \log N}{M}}. \end{equation} \end{claim}
nodes.statement_short: State Claim 7 on E|S| and gamma.

nodes.name: Expected size of S and choice of gamma
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} |S| \ge t_0 - \theta M, \end{equation} where \begin{equation*} \theta := 1080 \hat p^2 \mathbb I + \begin{cases} 6480\sqrt{\frac{2(C + 3)\log N}{p\hat n}}, &\quad p \le 0.49, \\ 6250\sqrt{\frac{(C + 3)\log N}{q^2\hat n } }\log \frac{\hat n}{\log N}, &\quad p > 0.49, \end{cases} \end{equation*} and, with $\gamma$ as in~\eqref{eq_gamma}, \begin{equation} \gamma \ge \tau_0 + \theta + 2/M + \sqrt{\frac{2C \log N}{M}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: E|S| >= t_0 - theta M, and gamma dominates tau_0 + theta + 2/M + sqrt(2C log N/M).
nodes.label: clm_sumofgammas

nodes.name: Lower bound on E|S|
nodes.statement: \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} |S| \ge t_0 - \theta M,
nodes.label: eq_theta_p

nodes.name: gamma dominates tau_0 + theta + error terms
nodes.statement: \gamma \ge \tau_0 + \theta + 2/M + \sqrt{\frac{2C \log N}{M}}.
nodes.label: eq_thetaM

nodes.name: Gap between E|S| and m
nodes.statement: Recalling that $t_0 = \lfloor (1 - \tau_0)M \rfloor$ and $m = \lceil(1-\gamma)M\rceil$, we have \begin{equation} \begin{split} t_0 - \theta M - m &\ge (1-\tau_0)M - 1 - \theta M - (1-\gamma)M - 1 \\ &= (\gamma - \tau_0 - \theta)M - 2 \By{\eqref{eq_thetaM}}{\ge} \sqrt{2C M \log N}. \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: t_0 - theta M - m >= sqrt(2CM log N).

nodes.name: Lower bound on t_0 - theta M - m
nodes.statement: \begin{split} t_0 - \theta M - m &\ge (1-\tau_0)M - 1 - \theta M - (1-\gamma)M - 1 \\ &= (\gamma - \tau_0 - \theta)M - 2 \By{\eqref{eq_thetaM}}{\ge} \sqrt{2C M \log N}. \end{split}
nodes.label: eq_tzero_theta_Mm

nodes.name: Chernoff for |S|
nodes.statement: Since $|S|$ is a sum of independent Bernoulli random variables, \begin{align*} \prob{|S| < m} &= \prob{|S| < \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|S|- (\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|S| - m) } \By{\eqref{eq_theta_p}}{\le} \prob{|S| < \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}|S| -(t_0 - \theta M - m)} \\ \justify{\eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}, $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}} |S| \le M$} &\By{}{\le} \exp \left( -\frac{(t_0 - \theta M - m)^2}{2M} \right) \By{\eqref{eq_tzero_theta_Mm}}{\le} \exp \left( - C \log N \right) = N^{-C}, \end{align*} which as mentioned above, implies~\eqref{eq_lower_embed}.
nodes.statement_short: Lower-tail Chernoff gives P(|S|<m) <= N^{-C}, proving eq_lower_embed.

nodes.name: Couple G(n1,n2,p') inside G(n1,n2,m)
nodes.statement: Finally, we prove~\eqref{eq:embed_Gnp} by coupling $\mathbb G(n_1, n_2, p')$ with $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2, m)$ so that the former is a subset of the latter with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$. Denote by $X := e(\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p'))$ the number of edges of $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2, p')$. Whenever $X \le m$, choose $X$ edges of $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$ at random and declare them to be a copy of $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p')$. Otherwise sample $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p')$ independently from $\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,m)$. Hence it remains to show that $\prob{X > m} = O(N^{-C})$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce eq:embed_Gnp to P(X>m) = O(N^{-C}).

nodes.name: Chernoff for X
nodes.statement: Recalling that $m = \ceil{(1-\gamma)}pN$ and $p' = (1 - 2\gamma)p$, we have $m/N \ge (1 - \gamma)p = p' + \gamma p$. Since $X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(N,p')$, Chernoff's bound~\eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} implies that \begin{equation} \prob{X > m} \le \prob{X > p'N + \gamma p N} \le \exp\left\{ -\frac{(\gamma pN)^2}{2(p'N + \gamma pN/3)} \right\} \le e^{-\gamma^2pN/2}. \end{equation} Choosing $C^*$ sufficiently large, the definition~\eqref{eq_gamma} implies $\gamma \ge \sqrt{\frac{2C\log N}{p N}}$ with a lot of room (to see this easier in the case $p > 0.49$, note that \eqref{eq:thm_embed_q} implies $\log(\hat n/\log N) \ge 1$, say). So~\eqref{eq:Xmorem} implies $\prob{X > m} \le N^{-C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Upper-tail Chernoff and gamma >= sqrt(2C log N/(pN)) give P(X>m) <= N^{-C}.

nodes.name: Tail bound P(X>m)
nodes.statement: \prob{X > m} \le \prob{X > p'N + \gamma p N} \le \exp\left\{ -\frac{(\gamma pN)^2}{2(p'N + \gamma pN/3)} \right\} \le e^{-\gamma^2pN/2}.
nodes.label: eq:Xmorem

nodes.name: Family R_{G,e,not f}
nodes.statement: For a graph~$G$ with $t$ edges and $e, f \in K\setminus G$, define \begin{equation*} {\mathcal{R}}_{G,e,\neg f} := \left\{ H \in {\mathcal{R}}_G : e \in H, f \notin H\right\}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Classes R and R' for the switching
nodes.statement: Recalling our generic definition of switchings from Subsection~\ref{ss_switchings}, let us treat the graphs in ${\mathcal{R}} := {\mathcal{R}}_{G,e,\neg f}$ and ${\mathcal{R}}' := {\mathcal{R}}_{G,f,\neg e}$ as blue-red edge colorings of the graph $K \setminus G$.

nodes.name: Switching graph B via alternating 6-cycles
nodes.statement: When edges $e,f$ are disjoint, we define the switching graph $B = B({\mathcal{R}},{\mathcal{R}}')$ by putting an edge between $H \in {\mathcal{R}}$ and $H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'$ whenever there is an alternating $6$-cycle containing $e$ and $f$ in $H$ such that switching the colors in the cycle gives $H'$ (see Figure~\ref{fig_coupling}). If $e$ and $f$ share a vertex, instead of $6$-cycles we use alternating $4$-cycles containing $e$ and $f$.

nodes.name: Alternating path count theta_{G,H}(u,v)
nodes.statement: For distinct $u,v\in V_i$, let $\theta_{G,H}(u,v)$ be the number of (alternating) paths $uxv$ such that $ux$ is blue and $xv$ is red.

nodes.name: Degrees in the switching graph B
nodes.statement: Then, setting $f = u_1u_2$ and $e = v_1v_2$, where $u_i,v_i\in V_i$, $i = 1,2$, \begin{equation} \deg_B(H) = \prod_{i: u_i \neq v_i}\theta_{G,H}(u_i,v_i), \quad H \in {\mathcal{R}} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \deg_B(H') = \prod_{i: u_i \neq v_i}\theta_{G,H'}(v_i,u_i), \quad H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Degrees in B are products of theta counts over the coordinates where e and f differ.

nodes.name: Forward degree in switching graph
nodes.statement: \deg_B(H) = \prod_{i: u_i \neq v_i}\theta_{G,H}(u_i,v_i), \quad H \in {\mathcal{R}}
nodes.label: eq_deg_forw

nodes.name: Backward degree in switching graph
nodes.statement: \deg_B(H') = \prod_{i: u_i \neq v_i}\theta_{G,H'}(v_i,u_i), \quad H' \in {\mathcal{R}}'.
nodes.label: eq_deg_back

nodes.name: Ratio |R|/|R'| via average degrees
nodes.statement: Note that equation~\eqref{eq_BRR} is equivalent to \begin{equation} \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|} = \frac{\frac1{|{\mathcal{R}}'|}\sum_{H'\in{\mathcal{R}}'}\deg_B(H')}{\frac1{|{\mathcal{R}}|}\sum_{H\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Ratio |R|/|R'| as ratio of average degrees
nodes.statement: \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|} = \frac{\frac1{|{\mathcal{R}}'|}\sum_{H'\in{\mathcal{R}}'}\deg_B(H')}{\frac1{|{\mathcal{R}}|}\sum_{H\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H)}.
nodes.label: eq_ratio_R

nodes.name: Heuristic for typical theta values
nodes.statement: To get an idea of how large that expectation could be, let us focus on one factor, say, $\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)$, assuming $u_1 \neq v_1$. Clearly, the red degree of $v_1$ equals $|\Gamma_{K\setminus\mathbb R}(v_1)| = n_2 - d_2 = qn_2$. Since $|\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(v_1)| = pn_2$, viewing $\mathbb R \setminus G$ as a $\tau$-dense subgraph of $\mathbb R$ (see \eqref{eq_tau}) we expect that the blue neighborhood $|\Gamma_{\mathbb R\setminus G}(u_1)|$ is approximately $\tau p n_2$. It is reasonable to expect that for typical $G$ and $\mathbb R$ the red and blue neighborhoods intersect proportionally, that is, on a set of size about $q \cdot \tau p \cdot n_2 = \tau qd_1$.

nodes.name: delta-typical graph
nodes.statement: Inspired by this heuristic, we say that, for $\delta > 0$, an admissible graph $G$ with $t$ edges is \emph{$\delta$-typical} if \begin{equation} \max_{u_1u_2, v_1v_2 \in K \setminus G} \Pc{\max_{i \in [2] : u_i \neq v_i}\left|\frac{\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i)}{\tau qd_i } - 1\right| > \delta }{G \subseteq \mathbb R, v_1v_2 \in \mathbb R, u_1u_2 \notin \mathbb R} \le \tau^2 \delta, \end{equation} where the outer maximum is taken over distinct pairs of edges.

nodes.name: delta-typicality condition
nodes.statement: \max_{u_1u_2, v_1v_2 \in K \setminus G} \Pc{\max_{i \in [2] : u_i \neq v_i}\left|\frac{\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i)}{\tau qd_i } - 1\right| > \delta }{G \subseteq \mathbb R, v_1v_2 \in \mathbb R, u_1u_2 \notin \mathbb R} \le \tau^2 \delta,
nodes.label: eq_typical

nodes.name: delta(t) and lambda(t)
nodes.statement: For each $t = 0, \dots, t_0 - 1$, define \begin{equation} \delta(t) := 120\hat p^2 \mathbb I + 360 \sqrt{\frac{(C + 3)\lambda(t)}{6\tau pq\hat n }} , \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \lambda(t) := \begin{cases} 6 \log N, \quad &p \le 0.49, \\ 6\log N + \frac{64\log N}{\tau p q}, \quad &p > 0.49. \end{cases} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of delta(t)
nodes.statement: \delta(t) := 120\hat p^2 \mathbb I + 360 \sqrt{\frac{(C + 3)\lambda(t)}{6\tau pq\hat n }} ,
nodes.label: eq_deltat

nodes.name: Definition of lambda(t)
nodes.statement: \lambda(t) := \begin{cases} 6 \log N, \quad &p \le 0.49, \\ 6\log N + \frac{64\log N}{\tau p q}, \quad &p > 0.49. \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq_lambda

nodes.name: delta(t) <= gamma_t/9
nodes.statement: For future reference, note that \begin{equation} \delta(t) \le \gamma_t/9. \end{equation}

nodes.name: delta(t) <= gamma_t/9
nodes.statement: \delta(t) \le \gamma_t/9.
nodes.label: eq_deltat_gammat

nodes.name: Proof that delta(t) <= gamma_t/9
nodes.statement: Indeed, recalling~\eqref{eq_gamma_t}, for $p\le0.49$, \[ 9\delta(t) \le 1080\hat p^2 \mathbb I + 3240 \sqrt{\frac{2(C + 3)\log N}{\tau p\hat n }} =\gamma_t, \] while, for $p > 0.49$, noting that $\lambda(t)\le 70\log N/(\tau pq)$, we have \[ 9\delta(t) \le 1080\hat p^2 \mathbb I + 3240 \sqrt{\frac{70(C + 3)\log N}{0.49^2 \cdot 6\tau^2q^2\hat n}} \le \gamma_t. \]
nodes.statement_short: Compare the definitions term by term in the two cases p<=0.49 and p>0.49.

nodes.name: Initial segments of R are typical
nodes.statement: For every constant $C > 0$, under the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}, \begin{equation*} \prob{\mathbb R(t) \text{ is } \delta(t)\text{-typical for all } t < t_0} = 1 - O(N^{-C}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: A.a.s. R(t) is delta(t)-typical for all t < t_0.
assumptions: For every constant $C > 0$, under the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw},
conclusions: \prob{\mathbb R(t) \text{ is } \delta(t)\text{-typical for all } t < t_0} = 1 - O(N^{-C}).
nodes.label: lem_typical

nodes.name: theta_t(u_i,v_i)
nodes.statement: For any $t = 0, \dots, M$ and distinct $u_i, v_i \in V_i$, $i = 1,2$, set \begin{equation} \theta_t(u_i,v_i) := \theta_{\mathbb R(t),\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i), \end{equation} where $\theta_{G,H}(u_i,v_i) = |\Gamma_{H\setminus G}(u_i)\cap\Gamma_{K\setminus H}(v_i)|$ was introduced earlier in this subsection.

nodes.name: theta_t(u_i,v_i) definition
nodes.statement: \theta_t(u_i,v_i) := \theta_{\mathbb R(t),\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i),
nodes.label: eq_theta_t

nodes.name: Conditional concentration of theta_t
nodes.statement: For every constant $C>0$, under the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}, for $i \in [2]$ we have that with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$, \begin{equation} \Pc{ \max_{u,v \in V_i, u \neq v} \left|\frac{\theta_t(u,v)}{\tau qd_{i} } - 1\right| > \delta(t)}{\mathbb R(t)} \le e^{ - 2\lambda(t) }, \qquad \text{for all } t < t_0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: With prob. 1-O(N^{-C}), for all t<t_0, conditionally on R(t) all theta_t(u,v)/(tau q d_i) are within delta(t) of 1 except with prob. e^{-2 lambda(t)}.
assumptions: For every constant $C>0$, under the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}, for $i \in [2]$
nodes.label: lem_thetas

nodes.name: Conditional concentration of theta_t
nodes.statement: \Pc{ \max_{u,v \in V_i, u \neq v} \left|\frac{\theta_t(u,v)}{\tau qd_{i} } - 1\right| > \delta(t)}{\mathbb R(t)} \le e^{ - 2\lambda(t) }, \qquad \text{for all } t < t_0.
nodes.label: eq_condthetas

nodes.name: Lower bound on P(e in R, f not in R | R(t))
nodes.statement: For every constant $C > 0$, under the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}, with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$ \begin{equation} \min_{e, f \in K \setminus \mathbb R(t), e \neq f}\Pc{e \in \mathbb R, f \notin \mathbb R}{\mathbb R(t)} \ge e^{ - \lambda(t) }, \qquad \text{for all } t < t_0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: With prob. 1-O(N^{-C}), for all t<t_0 and distinct e,f outside R(t), P(e in R, f not in R | R(t)) >= e^{-lambda(t)}.
assumptions: For every constant $C > 0$, under the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}
nodes.label: lem_ef

nodes.name: Lower bound on P(e in R, f not in R | R(t))
nodes.statement: \min_{e, f \in K \setminus \mathbb R(t), e \neq f}\Pc{e \in \mathbb R, f \notin \mathbb R}{\mathbb R(t)} \ge e^{ - \lambda(t) }, \qquad \text{for all } t < t_0.
nodes.label: eq_edgesNonnegligible

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement:
In view of Lemma~ef{lem_typical}, it suffices to show that if $t < t_0$, and a $t$-edge graph $G$ is $\delta(t)$-typical, then  egin{equation*} \min_{e \in K \setminus G}p_{t+1}(e,G) \ge  rac{1 - \gamma_t}{N - t}. \end{equation*} Fix $f \in K \setminus G$ which \emph{maximizes} $p_{t+1}(f,G)$. Since the average of $p_{t+1}(e,G)$ over $e \in K \setminus G$ is exactly $ rac{1}{N - t}$, we have $p_{t+1}(f,G) \ge  rac{1}{N - t}$ and therefore it is enough to prove that, for every $e \in K \setminus (G \cup \{f\})$,  egin{equation*}  rac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} \ge 1 - \gamma_t. \end{equation*} Recall the definitions of ${\mathcal{R}}_G$ in~\eqref{eq_rcG}, ${\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}, {\mathcal{R}}_{G, 
eg e}$ in~\eqref{eq_rcGe}, and ${\mathcal{R}} = {\mathcal{R}}_{G,e,
eg f}$ and ${\mathcal{R}}' = {\mathcal{R}}_{G, f, 
eg e}$ from Subsection ef{ss_prep} and observe that ${\mathcal{R}} = {\mathcal{R}}_{G\cup \{e\},
eg f}$ too. In view of the remark immediately following~\eqref{eq_pt},  egin{equation*} p_{t+1}(e,G) = \Pc{e \in \mathbb R}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \cdot \Pc{\eta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R(t) = G, e \in \mathbb R} =  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_G|} \cdot  rac{1}{M-t}. \end{equation*} Therefore,  egin{equation*} 1 \ge  rac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} =  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,f}|} =  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G \cup \{e,f\}}| + |{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e,
eg f}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G \cup \{e, f\}}| + |{\mathcal{R}}_{G,f,
eg e}| } \ge  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|}. \end{equation*} Write $e = v_1v_2$ and $f = u_1u_2$ and for simplicity assume that both $u_1 
eq v_1$ and $u_2 
eq v_2$ (otherwise the proof goes mutatis mutandis and is, in fact, a bit simpler). By~\eqref{eq_deg_forw},~\eqref{eq_deg_back}, and~\eqref{eq_ratio_R},  egin{equation*}  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|} =  rac{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{top}}}{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{bottom}}}, \end{equation*} where  egin{equation*} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{top}} :=  rac1{|{\mathcal{R}}'|}\sum_{H'\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H')= \Ec{	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(v_1,u_1)	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(v_2,u_2)}{G \subseteq \mathbb R, f \in \mathbb R, e 
otin \mathbb R} \end{equation*} and  egin{equation*} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{bottom}} :=  rac1{|{\mathcal{R}}|}\sum_{H\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H)= \Ec{	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_2,v_2)}{G \subseteq \mathbb R, e \in \mathbb R, f 
otin \mathbb R}. \end{equation*} Since $G$ is $\delta$-typical with $\delta = \delta(t)$, denoting the LHS{} of~\eqref{eq_typical} as $p_*$, we have $p_* \le 	au^2 \delta$, so  egin{align} 
otag \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{top}} &\ge (1 - \delta) 	au qd_1 \cdot (1 - \delta)	au qd_2 \cdot (1 - p_*) + 0 \cdot p_* \ &\ge (1 - \delta)^2 	au^2p^2q^2n_1n_2(1 - 	au^2\delta ) \ge (1 - \delta)^3 	au^2p^2q^2N. \end{align} Moreover, since, deterministically,  egin{equation*} 	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_1, v_1)	heta_{G, \mathbb R}(u_2, v_2) \le \min\{p,q\} n_2\cdot \min\{p,q\}n_1 \le 4p^2q^2N, \end{equation*} using~\eqref{eq_typical} again, we infer that  egin{align} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{bottom}} 
otag &\le (1 + \delta) 	au qd_1 \cdot (1 + \delta)	au qd_2 \cdot (1 - p_*) + 4p^2q^2N \cdot p^*\ &\le (1 + \delta)^2	au^2p^2q^2N + 4p^2q^2N \cdot 	au^2\delta \le (1 + 6\delta + \delta^2)	au^2p^2q^2N . \end{align} Finally, combining the bounds on $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{top}}$ and $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{bottom}}$ and using~\eqref{eq_deltat_gammat}, we conclude that  egin{equation}  rac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} \ge  rac{(1 - \delta)^3}{(1 + 6 \delta + \delta^2)} \ge 1 - 9\delta \ge 1 - \gamma_t, \end{equation} and the proof of Lemma~ef{lem_Stanislaw} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to typical G; express p_{t+1}(e,G)/p_{t+1}(f,G) via a 6-cycle switching and bound the expected switching degrees using typicality.

nodes.name: Reduce to typical G
nodes.statement: In view of Lemma~\ref{lem_typical}, it suffices to show that if $t < t_0$, and a $t$-edge graph $G$ is $\delta(t)$-typical, then \begin{equation*} \min_{e \in K \setminus G}p_{t+1}(e,G) \ge \frac{1 - \gamma_t}{N - t}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 8 it suffices to treat delta(t)-typical G.

nodes.name: Compare with the maximizing edge
nodes.statement: Fix $f \in K \setminus G$ which \emph{maximizes} $p_{t+1}(f,G)$. Since the average of $p_{t+1}(e,G)$ over $e \in K \setminus G$ is exactly $\frac{1}{N - t}$, we have $p_{t+1}(f,G) \ge \frac{1}{N - t}$ and therefore it is enough to prove that, for every $e \in K \setminus (G \cup \{f\})$, \begin{equation*} \frac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} \ge 1 - \gamma_t. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Take f maximizing p_{t+1}(f,G); suffices to bound the ratio for every e.

nodes.name: Express p_{t+1}(e,G)
nodes.statement:
Recall the definitions of ${\mathcal{R}}_G$ in~\eqref{eq_rcG}, ${\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}, {\mathcal{R}}_{G, 
eg e}$ in~\eqref{eq_rcGe}, and ${\mathcal{R}} = {\mathcal{R}}_{G,e,
eg f}$ and ${\mathcal{R}}' = {\mathcal{R}}_{G, f, 
eg e}$ from Subsection ef{ss_prep} and observe that ${\mathcal{R}} = {\mathcal{R}}_{G\cup \{e\},
eg f}$ too. In view of the remark immediately following~\eqref{eq_pt},  egin{equation*} p_{t+1}(e,G) = \Pc{e \in \mathbb R}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \cdot \Pc{\eta_{t+1} = e}{\mathbb R(t) = G, e \in \mathbb R} =  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_G|} \cdot  rac{1}{M-t}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Ratio bounded by |R|/|R'|
nodes.statement: Therefore, \begin{equation*} 1 \ge \frac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} = \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,f}|} = \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G \cup \{e,f\}}| + |{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e,\neg f}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G \cup \{e, f\}}| + |{\mathcal{R}}_{G,f,\neg e}| } \ge \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The ratio is at least |R_{G,e,not f}|/|R_{G,f,not e}|.

nodes.name: Ratio p_{t+1}(e,G)/p_{t+1}(f,G) >= |R|/|R'|
nodes.statement: 1 \ge \frac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} = \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G,f}|} = \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G \cup \{e,f\}}| + |{\mathcal{R}}_{G,e,\neg f}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{G \cup \{e, f\}}| + |{\mathcal{R}}_{G,f,\neg e}| } \ge \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|}.
nodes.label: eq_ratio

nodes.name: Ratio as E_top/E_bottom
nodes.statement:
Write $e = v_1v_2$ and $f = u_1u_2$ and for simplicity assume that both $u_1 
eq v_1$ and $u_2 
eq v_2$ (otherwise the proof goes mutatis mutandis and is, in fact, a bit simpler). By~\eqref{eq_deg_forw},~\eqref{eq_deg_back}, and~\eqref{eq_ratio_R},  egin{equation*}  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}|}{|{\mathcal{R}}'|} =  rac{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{top}}}{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{bottom}}}, \end{equation*} where  egin{equation*} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{top}} :=  rac1{|{\mathcal{R}}'|}\sum_{H'\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H')= \Ec{	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(v_1,u_1)	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(v_2,u_2)}{G \subseteq \mathbb R, f \in \mathbb R, e 
otin \mathbb R} \end{equation*} and  egin{equation*} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{	ext{bottom}} :=  rac1{|{\mathcal{R}}|}\sum_{H\in{\mathcal{R}}}\deg_B(H)= \Ec{	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_2,v_2)}{G \subseteq \mathbb R, e \in \mathbb R, f 
otin \mathbb R}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: By the switching degree formulas, |R|/|R'| = E_top/E_bottom.

nodes.name: Lower bound on E_top
nodes.statement: Since $G$ is $\delta$-typical with $\delta = \delta(t)$, denoting the LHS{} of~\eqref{eq_typical} as $p_*$, we have $p_* \le \tau^2 \delta$, so \begin{align} \notag \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{\text{top}} &\ge (1 - \delta) \tau qd_1 \cdot (1 - \delta)\tau qd_2 \cdot (1 - p_*) + 0 \cdot p_* \\ &\ge (1 - \delta)^2 \tau^2p^2q^2n_1n_2(1 - \tau^2\delta ) \ge (1 - \delta)^3 \tau^2p^2q^2N. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Typicality gives E_top >= (1-delta)^3 tau^2 p^2 q^2 N.

nodes.name: Lower bound on E_top
nodes.statement: \notag \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{\text{top}} &\ge (1 - \delta) \tau qd_1 \cdot (1 - \delta)\tau qd_2 \cdot (1 - p_*) + 0 \cdot p_* \\ &\ge (1 - \delta)^2 \tau^2p^2q^2n_1n_2(1 - \tau^2\delta ) \ge (1 - \delta)^3 \tau^2p^2q^2N.
nodes.label: eq_top_bound

nodes.name: Upper bound on E_bottom
nodes.statement: Moreover, since, deterministically, \begin{equation*} \theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_1, v_1)\theta_{G, \mathbb R}(u_2, v_2) \le \min\{p,q\} n_2\cdot \min\{p,q\}n_1 \le 4p^2q^2N, \end{equation*} using~\eqref{eq_typical} again, we infer that \begin{align} \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{\text{bottom}} \notag &\le (1 + \delta) \tau qd_1 \cdot (1 + \delta)\tau qd_2 \cdot (1 - p_*) + 4p^2q^2N \cdot p^*\\ &\le (1 + \delta)^2\tau^2p^2q^2N + 4p^2q^2N \cdot \tau^2\delta \le (1 + 6\delta + \delta^2)\tau^2p^2q^2N . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Typicality plus a deterministic bound give E_bottom <= (1+6delta+delta^2) tau^2 p^2 q^2 N.

nodes.name: Upper bound on E_bottom
nodes.statement: \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{\text{bottom}} \notag &\le (1 + \delta) \tau qd_1 \cdot (1 + \delta)\tau qd_2 \cdot (1 - p_*) + 4p^2q^2N \cdot p^*\\ &\le (1 + \delta)^2\tau^2p^2q^2N + 4p^2q^2N \cdot \tau^2\delta \le (1 + 6\delta + \delta^2)\tau^2p^2q^2N .
nodes.label: eq_bottom_bound

nodes.name: Conclude ratio >= 1 - gamma_t
nodes.statement: Finally, combining the bounds on $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{\text{top}}$ and $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_{\text{bottom}}$ and using~\eqref{eq_deltat_gammat}, we conclude that \begin{equation} \frac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} \ge \frac{(1 - \delta)^3}{(1 + 6 \delta + \delta^2)} \ge 1 - 9\delta \ge 1 - \gamma_t, \end{equation} and the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Combine and use delta(t) <= gamma_t/9.

nodes.name: p_{t+1}(e,G)/p_{t+1}(f,G) >= 1-gamma_t
nodes.statement: \frac{p_{t+1}(e,G)}{p_{t+1}(f,G)} \ge \frac{(1 - \delta)^3}{(1 + 6 \delta + \delta^2)} \ge 1 - 9\delta \ge 1 - \gamma_t,
nodes.label: eq_p_ratio

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement:
By Lemmas ef{lem_thetas} and ef{lem_ef} the events~\eqref{eq_condthetas} (for each $i \in [2]$) and~\eqref{eq_edgesNonnegligible} hold simultaneously with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$. Hence it suffices to fix an arbitrary integer $t < t_0$ and a realization of $\mathbb R(t)$, say $\mathbb R(t) = G$ satisfying inequalities~\eqref{eq_condthetas} (for each $i \in [2]$) and~\eqref{eq_edgesNonnegligible} and to prove that $G$ is $\delta(t)$-typical. Fix any such $G$ and define events  egin{equation*} {\mathcal{E}} :=  igcup_{i \in [2]} \left\{ \max_{u,v \in V_i, u 
eq v}\left| rac{	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u,v)}{	au qd_i } - 1ight| > \delta(t) ight\} \quad	ext{and}\quad {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f} := \{ e\in \mathbb R, f 
otin \mathbb R \}. \end{equation*} Since, conditioning on the event $\mathbb R(t) = G$, we have $	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i) = 	heta_t(u_i,v_i)$, by the choice of $G$ we have  egin{equation} \Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \le 2e^{-2\lambda(t)} \end{equation} and  egin{equation} \min_{e,f\in K \setminus G}\Pc{{\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \ge e^{-\lambda(t)}. \end{equation} Note that the probability on the LHS of~\eqref{eq_typical} does not change if we replace $G \subseteq \mathbb R$ by $\mathbb R(t) = G$, since conditioning on either event makes $\mathbb R$ uniformly distributed over ${\mathcal{R}}_G$ (i.e., biregular graphs containing $G$) and the random variables $	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i)$ do not depend on the random ordering of the edges of $\mathbb R$. Hence it remains to prove that~\eqref{eq_thetas_Rt} and~\eqref{eq_edges_Rt} imply, for any distinct edges $e = v_1v_2, f = u_1u_2 \in K \setminus G$, that  egin{equation} \Pc{\max_{i \in [2] : u_i 
eq v_i}\left| rac{	heta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i)}{	au qd_i } - 1ight| > \delta(t) }{\mathbb R(t) = G, e \in \mathbb R, f 
otin \mathbb R} \le 	au^2 \delta(t). \end{equation} The probability on the {LHS} of~\eqref{eq_typical2} is at most $\Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G, {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}$. Inequalities~\eqref{eq_thetas_Rt} and~\eqref{eq_edges_Rt} imply that  egin{equation*} \Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G, {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}} =  rac{\Pc{{\mathcal{E}}\cap {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}}{\Pc{{\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}} \le  rac{\Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}}{\Pc{{\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}} \le 2 e^{ - \lambda(t)}. \end{equation*} Finally, even a quick glance at the definitions of $\delta(t)$ and $	au_0$ (see~\eqref{eq_deltat} and~\eqref{eq_tauzero}) reveals that $\min \{ 	au_0,\delta(t) \} \ge 1/\hat n$. Thus, we get, with a huge margin,  egin{equation*} 2e^{-\lambda(t)}\le 2/N^6 \le 1/N^2 \le 1/\hat n^4 \le 	au_0^2\delta(t) \le 	au^2\delta(t). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the conditional probability of atypical theta by the ratio of the Lemma 9 and Lemma 10 probabilities.

nodes.name: Reduce to a fixed good G
nodes.statement: By Lemmas \ref{lem_thetas} and \ref{lem_ef} the events~\eqref{eq_condthetas} (for each $i \in [2]$) and~\eqref{eq_edgesNonnegligible} hold simultaneously with probability $1 - O(N^{-C})$. Hence it suffices to fix an arbitrary integer $t < t_0$ and a realization of $\mathbb R(t)$, say $\mathbb R(t) = G$ satisfying inequalities~\eqref{eq_condthetas} (for each $i \in [2]$) and~\eqref{eq_edgesNonnegligible} and to prove that $G$ is $\delta(t)$-typical.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemmas 9 and 10 it suffices to show a fixed good G is typical.

nodes.name: Define events E and F_{e,f}
nodes.statement: Fix any such $G$ and define events \begin{equation*} {\mathcal{E}} := \bigcup_{i \in [2]} \left\{ \max_{u,v \in V_i, u \neq v}\left|\frac{\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u,v)}{\tau qd_i } - 1\right| > \delta(t) \right\} \quad\text{and}\quad {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f} := \{ e\in \mathbb R, f \notin \mathbb R \}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define the atypical event E and F_{e,f} = {e in R, f not in R}.

nodes.name: Bounds from the choice of G
nodes.statement: Since, conditioning on the event $\mathbb R(t) = G$, we have $\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i) = \theta_t(u_i,v_i)$, by the choice of $G$ we have \begin{equation} \Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \le 2e^{-2\lambda(t)} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \min_{e,f\in K \setminus G}\Pc{{\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \ge e^{-\lambda(t)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: P(E|R(t)=G) <= 2e^{-2 lambda(t)} and P(F_{e,f}|R(t)=G) >= e^{-lambda(t)}.

nodes.name: P(E | R(t)=G) <= 2e^{-2 lambda(t)}
nodes.statement: \Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \le 2e^{-2\lambda(t)}
nodes.label: eq_thetas_Rt

nodes.name: min P(F_{e,f} | R(t)=G) >= e^{-lambda(t)}
nodes.statement: \min_{e,f\in K \setminus G}\Pc{{\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G} \ge e^{-\lambda(t)}.
nodes.label: eq_edges_Rt

nodes.name: Reduce to eq_typical2
nodes.statement: Note that the probability on the LHS of~\eqref{eq_typical} does not change if we replace $G \subseteq \mathbb R$ by $\mathbb R(t) = G$, since conditioning on either event makes $\mathbb R$ uniformly distributed over ${\mathcal{R}}_G$ (i.e., biregular graphs containing $G$) and the random variables $\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i)$ do not depend on the random ordering of the edges of $\mathbb R$. Hence it remains to prove that~\eqref{eq_thetas_Rt} and~\eqref{eq_edges_Rt} imply, for any distinct edges $e = v_1v_2, f = u_1u_2 \in K \setminus G$, that \begin{equation} \Pc{\max_{i \in [2] : u_i \neq v_i}\left|\frac{\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i)}{\tau qd_i } - 1\right| > \delta(t) }{\mathbb R(t) = G, e \in \mathbb R, f \notin \mathbb R} \le \tau^2 \delta(t). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Conditioning on G subset R equals conditioning on R(t)=G; remains to prove eq_typical2.

nodes.name: Typicality inequality given R(t)=G
nodes.statement: \Pc{\max_{i \in [2] : u_i \neq v_i}\left|\frac{\theta_{G,\mathbb R}(u_i,v_i)}{\tau qd_i } - 1\right| > \delta(t) }{\mathbb R(t) = G, e \in \mathbb R, f \notin \mathbb R} \le \tau^2 \delta(t).
nodes.label: eq_typical2

nodes.name: Bound by a ratio
nodes.statement: The probability on the {LHS} of~\eqref{eq_typical2} is at most $\Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G, {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}$. Inequalities~\eqref{eq_thetas_Rt} and~\eqref{eq_edges_Rt} imply that \begin{equation*} \Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G, {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}} = \frac{\Pc{{\mathcal{E}}\cap {\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}}{\Pc{{\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}} \le \frac{\Pc{{\mathcal{E}}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}}{\Pc{{\mathcal{F}}_{e,f}}{\mathbb R(t) = G}} \le 2 e^{ - \lambda(t)}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: P(E | R(t)=G, F_{e,f}) <= 2 e^{-lambda(t)}.

nodes.name: Compare with tau^2 delta(t)
nodes.statement: Finally, even a quick glance at the definitions of $\delta(t)$ and $\tau_0$ (see~\eqref{eq_deltat} and~\eqref{eq_tauzero}) reveals that $\min \{ \tau_0,\delta(t) \} \ge 1/\hat n$. Thus, we get, with a huge margin, \begin{equation*} 2e^{-\lambda(t)}\le 2/N^6 \le 1/N^2 \le 1/\hat n^4 \le \tau_0^2\delta(t) \le \tau^2\delta(t). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: 2e^{-lambda(t)} <= tau^2 delta(t) with a huge margin.

nodes.name: Co-degree
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{co-degree} of two distinct vertices $u, v$ as \begin{equation} \operatorname{cod}_F(u,v) := |\Gamma_F(u) \cap \Gamma_F(v)|. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph

nodes.name: Co-degree definition
nodes.statement: \operatorname{cod}_F(u,v) := |\Gamma_F(u) \cap \Gamma_F(v)|.
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.label: eq_def_cod

nodes.name: Co-degree complement identity
nodes.statement: A few times we will use the following simple observation: for $F \subseteq K$ and distinct $u,v\in V_1$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} \operatorname{cod}_{F}(u, v) &= |\Gamma_{F}(u)| + |\Gamma_{F}(v)| - |\Gamma_{F}(u) \cup \Gamma_{F}(v)| \\ &= \deg_F(u) + \deg_F(v) - \left( n_2 - \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus F}(u,v) \right), \end{split} \end{equation} where, recall, $K = K_{n_1,n_2}$ is the complete bipartite graph.
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement_short: cod_F(u,v) = deg_F(u)+deg_F(v) - (n_2 - cod_{K minus F}(u,v)).

nodes.name: Co-degree complement identity
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \operatorname{cod}_{F}(u, v) &= |\Gamma_{F}(u)| + |\Gamma_{F}(v)| - |\Gamma_{F}(u) \cup \Gamma_{F}(v)| \\ &= \deg_F(u) + \deg_F(v) - \left( n_2 - \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus F}(u,v) \right), \end{split}
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph

nodes.name: Co-degree concentration in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\hat p\hat n \to \infty$ and let $\lambda = \lambda(n_1,n_2)$ be such that $\lambda \to \infty$. Then, for any distinct $u_1, v_1 \in V_1$, \begin{equation*} \prob{ |\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1) - p^2n_{2}| > 20\left( \hat p^3n_{2}\mathbb I + \frac{\hat pn_{2}}{\hat n} + \sqrt{\lambda \hat p^2 n_2} \right) + \lambda } = O\left( \sqrt N e^{ - \lambda } \right), \end{equation*} where $\mathbb I$ is defined in~\eqref{eq_defI}.
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement_short: cod_R(u_1,v_1) deviates from p^2 n_2 by more than 20(p-hat^3 n_2 I + p-hat n_2/n-hat + sqrt(lambda p-hat^2 n_2)) + lambda with prob. O(sqrt(N) e^{-lambda}).
assumptions: Suppose that $\hat p\hat n  \to \infty$  and let $\lambda = \lambda(n_1,n_2)$ be such that $\lambda \to \infty$.
