nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 11
nodes.statement:
We first claim that it is sufficient to assume $p \le 1/2$ and prove that for any distinct $u_1, v_1 \in V_1$  egin{equation} \prob{ |\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1) - p^2n_2| > 20\left(p^3n_2\mathbb I +  rac{pn_2}{\hat n} + \sqrt{\lambda p^2n_2 } ight) + \lambda } = O\left( \sqrt N e^{ - \lambda } ight). \end{equation} To see this, note that by~\eqref{eq_coco}, recalling $q = 1 - p$,  egin{equation*} \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1, v_1) - p^2n_2= 2pn_2 - (n_2 - \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R}(u_1,v_1))- p^2n_2=\operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R}(u_1,v_1) - q^2n_2. \end{equation*} Further, $K \setminus \mathbb R = K \setminus \mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$ has the same distribution as $\mathbb R(n_1,n_2,q)$. So, if $p > 1/2$, the lemma follows by applying~\eqref{eq_codegconcnoq} with $q$ instead of $p$. The crude proof idea comes from our anticipation that $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)$ behaves similarly to $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p)}(u_1,v_1)$, which is distributed as $\operatorname{Bin}(n_2, p^2)$ or, approximately, as $\operatorname{Po}(p^2n_2)$. We will show that each tail of $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,u_2)$ is comparable to the tail of $\operatorname{Po}(\mu)$ with expectation~$\mu$ fairly close to $p^2n_2$ and then apply the Chernoff bounds (this is packaged in Claim~ef{clm_Poiss_bounds} below). Further we consider the cases $\mathbb I = 1$ and $\mathbb I = 0$ and apply Claim~ef{clm_Poiss_bounds} analogously to the proof of Theorem 2.1 in~\cite{KSVW}: in the case $\mathbb I = 1$ we use switchings and in the case $\mathbb I = 0$ we use asymptotic enumeration (Theorem~ef{thm_enum}). Fix distinct $u_1, v_1 \in V_1$ and set $X(u_1,v_1): = \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)$. Further, recall that ${\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)$ is the class of subgraphs of $K_{n_1,n_2}$ such that every $v \in V_i$ has degree $d_i$, for $i = 1, 2$, and let \[ {\mathcal{R}}_k(u_1,v_1) = \{H \in {\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p) : \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1) = k \}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, d_1. \]  egin{claim} Fix two vertices $u_1,v_1\in V_1$. Suppose that positive numbers $r_k, k = 0, \dots, d_1,$ are such that  egin{equation*} |{\mathcal{R}}_k(u_1,v_1)| \sim r_k, 	ext{ uniformly in $k$ as } (n_1, n_2) 	o \infty, \end{equation*} and there exist numbers $0 \le \mu_- \le \mu_+ \le N$ such that  egin{equation*}  rac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} \le  rac{\mu_+}{k}, 	ext{ for } k \in [\mu_+, d_1] \quad 	ext{ and } \quad  rac{r_{k-1}}{r_k} \le  rac{k}{\mu_-}, 	ext{ for } k \in [1, \mu_-]. \end{equation*} If $x \ge \sqrt{2\mu_+ \lambda} + \lambda$, then  egin{equation} \prob{X(u_1,v_1) \ge \mu_+ + x} + \prob{X(u_1,v_1) \le \mu_- - x} = O(\sqrt{N} e^{-\lambda}). \end{equation} \end{claim}  egin{proof} Note that if $Z_+ \sim \operatorname{Po}(\mu_+)$, then $\mu_+/k = \prob{Z_+ = k}/\prob{Z_+ = k - 1}$. Setting $m = \lfloor \mu_+ floor$, for any integer $i\in\{m,\dots,d_1\}$, and abbreviating $X:=X(u_1,v_1)$ and ${\mathcal{R}}_j:={\mathcal{R}}_j(u_1,v_1)$, we have  egin{align*} \prob{X \ge i} &=  rac{\sum_{j \ge i}|{\mathcal{R}}_j| }{|{\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)|}\le \sum_{j \ge i}  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}_j|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{m}|} \sim \sum_{j \ge i}  rac{r_j}{r_m} = \sum_{j \ge i} \prod_{k = m + 1}^{j}  rac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} \le \sum_{j \ge i} \prod_{k = m + 1}^{j}  rac{\mu_+}{k}\ &= \sum_{j \ge i} \prod_{k = m + 1}^{j} rac{\prob{Z_+ = k}}{\prob{Z_+ = k-1}} = \sum_{j \ge i}  rac{\prob{Z_+ = j}}{\prob{Z_+ = m}} =  rac{\prob{Z_+ \ge i}}{\prob{Z_+ = m}}. \end{align*} Since $\mu_+ \le N$, by \eqref{eq_largestatom} we have $\prob{Z_+ = m} = \Omega(1/\sqrt{\mu_+}) = \Omega(1/\sqrt{N})$, and conclude that  egin{equation} \prob{X \ge i} = O\left( \sqrt{N} \cdot \prob{Z_+ \ge i} ight), \qquad i \ge \mu_+. \end{equation} Similarly, if $Z_- \sim \operatorname{Po}(\mu_-)$, then for $i\le m := \lfloor \mu_- floor$, using $k/\mu_- = \prob{Z_- = k-1}/\prob{Z_- = k}$,  egin{equation*} \prob{X \le i}\le \sum_{j \le i}  rac{|{\mathcal{R}}_j|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{m}|} \sim \sum_{j \le i}\prod_{k = j + 1}^{ m}  rac{r_{k-1}}{r_{k}} \le \sum_{j \le i}\prod_{k = j + 1}^{ m}  rac{\prob{Z_- = k-1}}{\prob{Z_- = k}} =  rac{\prob{Z_- \le i}}{\prob{Z_- = m}}, \end{equation*} and therefore, again using \eqref{eq_largestatom},  egin{equation} \prob{X \le i} = O\left( \sqrt{N} \cdot \prob{Z_- \le i} ight), \qquad i \le \mu_-. \end{equation} Since the RHS{} of \eqref{eq_twotailbound} does not depend on $x$, we can assume the equality: $x = \sqrt{2\mu_+\lambda} + \lambda$. Inequalities \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} and $\eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}$ imply  egin{equation*}  egin{split} \prob{Z_+ \ge \mu_+ + x} &+ \prob{Z_- \le \mu_- - x} \le \exp \left( -  rac{x^2}{2(\mu_+ + x/3)} ight) + \exp \left( - rac{x^2}{2\mu_-} ight) \ \justify{$\mu_- \le \mu_+, x > 0$} &\le 2 \exp \left( - rac{x^2}{2(\mu_+ + x/3)} ight) \ \justify{$x = \sqrt{2 \mu_+ \lambda} + \lambda$} &= 2 \exp \left( - rac{\lambda(2\mu_+ + 2\sqrt{2\mu_+ \lambda} + \lambda)}{2\mu_+ + \sqrt{2\mu_+ \lambda}/3 + \lambda/3} ight) \le 2e^{-\lambda}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Combining this with \eqref{eq_Poisstail_up} and \eqref{eq_Poisstail_down} yields \eqref{eq_twotailbound}. \end{proof} It remains to prove \eqref{eq_codegconcnoq}. We consider separately the cases $\mathbb I = 1$ and $\mathbb I = 0$. \smallskip 	extbf{Case $\mathbb I = 1$.} If $p \ge 1/5$, then deterministically $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,u_2) \le pn_2\le 5p^2n_2 \le p^2 n_2 + 20 p^3 n_2$ and $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1, u_2) - p^2 n_2 \ge - p^2 n_2 \ge -5p^3 n_2$, and hence \eqref{eq_codegconcnoq} holds trivially. nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to p<=1/2 by complements; compare co-degree tails with Poisson tails (Claim 12), using switchings when I=1 and the CGM enumeration when I=0.

nodes.name: Reduce to p <= 1/2
nodes.statement: We first claim that it is sufficient to assume $p \le 1/2$ and prove that for any distinct $u_1, v_1 \in V_1$ \begin{equation} \prob{ |\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1) - p^2n_2| > 20\left(p^3n_2\mathbb I + \frac{pn_2}{\hat n} + \sqrt{\lambda p^2n_2 } \right) + \lambda } = O\left( \sqrt N e^{ - \lambda } \right). \end{equation} To see this, note that by~\eqref{eq_coco}, recalling $q = 1 - p$, \begin{equation*} \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1, v_1) - p^2n_2= 2pn_2 - (n_2 - \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R}(u_1,v_1))- p^2n_2=\operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R}(u_1,v_1) - q^2n_2. \end{equation*} Further, $K \setminus \mathbb R = K \setminus \mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$ has the same distribution as $\mathbb R(n_1,n_2,q)$. So, if $p > 1/2$, the lemma follows by applying~\eqref{eq_codegconcnoq} with $q$ instead of $p$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph

nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.label: eq_codegconcnoq

nodes.name: Proof idea
nodes.statement: The crude proof idea comes from our anticipation that $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)$ behaves similarly to $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p)}(u_1,v_1)$, which is distributed as $\operatorname{Bin}(n_2, p^2)$ or, approximately, as $\operatorname{Po}(p^2n_2)$. We will show that each tail of $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,u_2)$ is comparable to the tail of $\operatorname{Po}(\mu)$ with expectation~$\mu$ fairly close to $p^2n_2$ and then apply the Chernoff bounds (this is packaged in Claim~\ref{clm_Poiss_bounds} below). Further we consider the cases $\mathbb I = 1$ and $\mathbb I = 0$ and apply Claim~\ref{clm_Poiss_bounds} analogously to the proof of Theorem 2.1 in~\cite{KSVW}: in the case $\mathbb I = 1$ we use switchings and in the case $\mathbb I = 0$ we use asymptotic enumeration (Theorem~\ref{thm_enum}).
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement_short: Compare co-degree tails with Poisson tails; switchings for I=1, enumeration for I=0.

nodes.name: Define X and R_k
nodes.statement: Fix distinct $u_1, v_1 \in V_1$ and set $X(u_1,v_1): = \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)$. Further, recall that ${\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)$ is the class of subgraphs of $K_{n_1,n_2}$ such that every $v \in V_i$ has degree $d_i$, for $i = 1, 2$, and let \[ {\mathcal{R}}_k(u_1,v_1) = \{H \in {\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p) : \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1) = k \}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, d_1. \]
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement_short: X = cod_R(u_1,v_1); R_k = graphs with co-degree k.

nodes.name: Claim 12 and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{claim} Fix two vertices $u_1,v_1\in V_1$. Suppose that positive numbers $r_k, k = 0, \dots, d_1,$ are such that \begin{equation*} |{\mathcal{R}}_k(u_1,v_1)| \sim r_k, \text{ uniformly in $k$ as } (n_1, n_2) \to \infty, \end{equation*} and there exist numbers $0 \le \mu_- \le \mu_+ \le N$ such that \begin{equation*} \frac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} \le \frac{\mu_+}{k}, \text{ for } k \in [\mu_+, d_1] \quad \text{ and } \quad \frac{r_{k-1}}{r_k} \le \frac{k}{\mu_-}, \text{ for } k \in [1, \mu_-]. \end{equation*} If $x \ge \sqrt{2\mu_+ \lambda} + \lambda$, then \begin{equation} \prob{X(u_1,v_1) \ge \mu_+ + x} + \prob{X(u_1,v_1) \le \mu_- - x} = O(\sqrt{N} e^{-\lambda}). \end{equation} \end{claim} \begin{proof} Note that if $Z_+ \sim \operatorname{Po}(\mu_+)$, then $\mu_+/k = \prob{Z_+ = k}/\prob{Z_+ = k - 1}$. Setting $m = \lfloor \mu_+ \rfloor$, for any integer $i\in\{m,\dots,d_1\}$, and abbreviating $X:=X(u_1,v_1)$ and ${\mathcal{R}}_j:={\mathcal{R}}_j(u_1,v_1)$, we have \begin{align*} \prob{X \ge i} &= \frac{\sum_{j \ge i}|{\mathcal{R}}_j| }{|{\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)|}\le \sum_{j \ge i} \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}_j|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{m}|} \sim \sum_{j \ge i} \frac{r_j}{r_m} = \sum_{j \ge i} \prod_{k = m + 1}^{j} \frac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} \le \sum_{j \ge i} \prod_{k = m + 1}^{j} \frac{\mu_+}{k}\\ &= \sum_{j \ge i} \prod_{k = m + 1}^{j}\frac{\prob{Z_+ = k}}{\prob{Z_+ = k-1}} = \sum_{j \ge i} \frac{\prob{Z_+ = j}}{\prob{Z_+ = m}} = \frac{\prob{Z_+ \ge i}}{\prob{Z_+ = m}}. \end{align*} Since $\mu_+ \le N$, by \eqref{eq_largestatom} we have $\prob{Z_+ = m} = \Omega(1/\sqrt{\mu_+}) = \Omega(1/\sqrt{N})$, and conclude that \begin{equation} \prob{X \ge i} = O\left( \sqrt{N} \cdot \prob{Z_+ \ge i} \right), \qquad i \ge \mu_+. \end{equation} Similarly, if $Z_- \sim \operatorname{Po}(\mu_-)$, then for $i\le m := \lfloor \mu_- \rfloor$, using $k/\mu_- = \prob{Z_- = k-1}/\prob{Z_- = k}$, \begin{equation*} \prob{X \le i}\le \sum_{j \le i} \frac{|{\mathcal{R}}_j|}{|{\mathcal{R}}_{m}|} \sim \sum_{j \le i}\prod_{k = j + 1}^{ m} \frac{r_{k-1}}{r_{k}} \le \sum_{j \le i}\prod_{k = j + 1}^{ m} \frac{\prob{Z_- = k-1}}{\prob{Z_- = k}} = \frac{\prob{Z_- \le i}}{\prob{Z_- = m}}, \end{equation*} and therefore, again using \eqref{eq_largestatom}, \begin{equation} \prob{X \le i} = O\left( \sqrt{N} \cdot \prob{Z_- \le i} \right), \qquad i \le \mu_-. \end{equation} Since the RHS{} of \eqref{eq_twotailbound} does not depend on $x$, we can assume the equality: $x = \sqrt{2\mu_+\lambda} + \lambda$. Inequalities \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} and $\eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}$ imply \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \prob{Z_+ \ge \mu_+ + x} &+ \prob{Z_- \le \mu_- - x} \le \exp \left( - \frac{x^2}{2(\mu_+ + x/3)} \right) + \exp \left( -\frac{x^2}{2\mu_-} \right) \\ \justify{$\mu_- \le \mu_+, x > 0$} &\le 2 \exp \left( -\frac{x^2}{2(\mu_+ + x/3)} \right) \\ \justify{$x = \sqrt{2 \mu_+ \lambda} + \lambda$} &= 2 \exp \left( -\frac{\lambda(2\mu_+ + 2\sqrt{2\mu_+ \lambda} + \lambda)}{2\mu_+ + \sqrt{2\mu_+ \lambda}/3 + \lambda/3} \right) \le 2e^{-\lambda}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Combining this with \eqref{eq_Poisstail_up} and \eqref{eq_Poisstail_down} yields \eqref{eq_twotailbound}. \end{proof}

By symmetry, the total number of bad choices is at most $2d_1d_2^2$, whence  egin{align*} \deg_{B_k}(H')/(d_1 - k + 1)^2 &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1)(d_2)_2 - 2d_1d_2^2 \ \justify{$k \ge 1$} &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1)d_2^2\left( 1 -  rac{1}{d_2} -  rac{2d_1}{n_2 - 2d_1} ight) \ \justify{$d_1 = n_2p, p \le 1/5$} &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1)d_2^2\left( 1- d_2^{-1} - 4p ight). \end{align*} Since, by our assumptions, $d_2 \ge \hat p\hat n 	o \infty$ and $p \le 1/5$, it follows that the graphs $B_k$ for $k = 1, \dots, d_1$ have minimum degrees at least $1$. Since we implicitly assume ${\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)$ is non-empty, this implies that all classes ${\mathcal{R}}_k, k = 0, \dots, d_1,$ are non-empty, i.e., the numbers $r_k = |{\mathcal{R}}_k|$ are all positive, satisfying one of the conditions of Claim~ef{clm_Poiss_bounds}. Using \eqref{eq_countingedges} and bounds on the degrees in $B_k$, for $k = 1, \dots, d_1,$ we have  egin{align} 
otag  rac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} \le  rac{\max_{H' \in {\mathcal{R}}' }\deg_{B_k}(H')}{\min_{H \in {\mathcal{R}}} \deg_{B_k}(H)} &\le  rac{(d_1 - k + 1)^2}{k(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)}\cdot rac{1}{1 - 4p} \ &\le  rac{(d_1 - k + 1)^2}{k(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)} \cdot \left( 1 + 20p ight), \end{align} (where the last inequality holds because $p \le 1/5$ implies $ rac{1}{1 - 4p} = 1 +  rac{4p}{1 - 4p} \le 1 + 20p$), and  egin{equation}  rac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} \ge  rac{\min_{H' \in {\mathcal{R}}' }\deg_{B_k}(H')}{\max_{H \in {\mathcal{R}}} \deg_{B_k}(H)} \ge  rac{(d_1 - 2d_1 + \mu)} \cdot  rac{\mu}{k} =  rac{\mu_+}{k}. \end{equation*} On the other hand, from \eqref{eq_rkLow}, \eqref{eq_mu_ratio}, and \eqref{eq_mupm} that, for $1\le k \le \mu$, we have  egin{equation*}  rac{r_{k-1}}{r_k} \le  rac{\mu (n_2 - 2d_1 + \mu)}{(d_1 - \mu + 1)^2\left( 1 - 1/d_2 -4p ight)} \cdot  rac{k}{\mu} =  rac{k}{\mu_-}. \end{equation*} Note that, since $\min\{d_1,d_2\} = p\hat n 	o \infty$ and $p\le1/5$, it follows by \eqref{eq_mu_np_square}, and \eqref{eq_mupm} that  egin{equation} p^2n_2(1 - 20\left(p^3n_2 +  rac{pn_2}{\hat n} ight). \end{equation} Consequently, setting  egin{equation} x := 20 \sqrt{\lambda p^2 n_2} + \lambda, \end{equation} we have, by \eqref{eq_mu_pm_bounds}  egin{equation*} \prob{|X - p^2n_2| \ge 20\left(p^3n_2 +  rac{pn_2}{\hat n}ight) + x} \le \prob{X \ge \mu_+ + x} + \prob{X\le \mu_- - x}. \end{equation*} Noting that the last inequality in \eqref{eq_mu_pm_ptwon} implies $x \ge \sqrt{\mu_+n_2} + \lambda $, using Claim~ef{clm_Poiss_bounds} we obtain~\eqref{eq_codegconcnoq}, completing the proof in the case $\mathbb I = 1$.

nodes.statement_short: Bound r_k/r_{k-1} via switchings and apply Claim 12.

nodes.name: Subcase p >= 1/5 trivial
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case $\mathbb I = 1$.} If $p \ge 1/5$, then deterministically $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,u_2) \le pn_2\le 5p^2n_2 \le p^2 n_2 + 20 p^3 n_2$ and $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1, u_2) - p^2 n_2 \ge - p^2 n_2 \ge -5p^3 n_2$, and hence \eqref{eq_codegconcnoq} holds trivially. So we further assume $p < 1/5$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement_short: For p >= 1/5 the bound holds deterministically; assume p < 1/5.

nodes.name: Define the co-degree switching
nodes.statement: Setting $r_k = |{\mathcal{R}}_k|$, we are going to prove bounds on $r_k/r_{k-1}$, $k\ge 1$, using a switching between ${\mathcal{R}} = {\mathcal{R}}_k$ and ${\mathcal{R}}' = {\mathcal{R}}_{k-1}$. To this end, recall our terminology from Subsection~\ref{ss_switchings} (with $G = \emptyset$): any graph $H \subseteq K$ is interpreted as a coloring of the edges of $K$, with the edges in $H$ blue and the rest red. We define a forward switching as follows: pick a common blue neighbor $w_2 \in \Gamma_H(u_1) \cap \Gamma_H(v_1)$ and find two alternating $4$-cycles $u_1w_2x_1x_2$ and $v_1w_2y_1y_2$ so that $x_1 \neq y_1$, $x_2 \neq y_2$. Moreover, we restrict the choice of the cycles to those for which $v_1x_2$ and $u_1y_2$ are red; this is to make sure that swapping of the colors on each of the two cycles (but keeping the color of $v_1x_2,u_1y_2$ red) indeed decreases $\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R}(u_1,v_1)$ by one, thus mapping $H \in {\mathcal{R}}_k$ to $H' \in {\mathcal{R}}_{k-1}$ (see Figure~\ref{fig_codegree}).
nodes.section: 5.1 Co-degrees in the random biregular graph
nodes.statement_short: Switch two alternating 4-cycles through a common neighbor w_2 to lower the co-degree by one.

nodes.name: Upper bound on forward degree
nodes.statement: Let $B_k := B({\mathcal{R}}_k, {\mathcal{R}}_{k-1})$ be the auxiliary graph corresponding to the described switching. Since the number of choices of $w_2$ is $k$ for any $H \in {\mathcal{R}}_k$, we will show upper and lower bounds on $\deg_{B_k}(H)/k$ by fixing $w_2$ and proving upper and lower bounds on the possible choices of $(x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2)$. For the upper bound, since there are $n_2 - 2d_1 + k$ common red neighbors of $u_1$ and $v_1$ (one can use \eqref{eq_coco} for this), the number of choices of distinct $x_2, y_2$ is exactly $(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2$, while the number of choices of $x_1$ and $y_1$, as blue neighbors of, resp., $x_2$ and $y_2$, is at most~$d_2^2$. Ignoring the requirements that $x_1\neq y_1$ and that both $x_1w_2$ and $y_1w_2$ should be red), we have shown \begin{equation} \deg_{B_k}(H)/k \le (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2d_2^2. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Lower bound on forward degree
nodes.statement: For the lower bound, we subtract from the upper bound \eqref{eq_degB_upper} the number of choices of $(x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2)$ for which either $x_1 = y_1$ or at least one of $x_1w_2$ and $y_1w_2$ is blue (the assumption $x_2 \neq y_2$ was taken into account in the upper bound). The number of choices with $x_1 = y_1$ is at most $n_1d_1^2$, and those with, say, $x_1w_2$ blue, is at most $d_2d_1 \cdot (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)d_2 $. Indeed, there are $\deg_H(w_2) \le d_2$ candidates for $x_1$ and, then, at most $d_1$ candidates for $x_2$, $\operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus H}(u_1,u_2) = n_2 - 2d_1 + k$ candidates for $y_2$, and then $d_2$ choices of $y_1$. Therefore \begin{align*} \deg_{B_k}(H)/k &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2d_2^2 - n_1d_1^2 - 2(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)d_1d_2^2 \\ &= (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2 d_2^2 \left( 1 - \frac{n_1d_1^2}{(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2 d_2^2} - \frac{2d_1}{n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1}\right) \\ \justify{$d_1 = n_2p, d_2 = n_1p, k \ge 1$}& \ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2 d_2^2 \left( 1 - \frac{n_2^2}{(n_2 - 2pn_2)^2 n_1} - \frac{2pn_2}{n_2 - 2pn_2}\right) \\ &= (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2 d_2^2 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{(1 - 2p)^2n_1} - \frac{2p}{1 - 2p}\right) \\ \justify{$p\le1/5$} &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2 d_2^2 \left( 1 - \left( \frac{25}{9pn_1} + \frac{10}{3} \right) p \right) \\ \justify{$\hat p \hat n \to \infty$} &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k)_2 d_2^2 \left( 1 - 4p \right). \end{align*}

nodes.statement_short: Subtract bad choices: deg_{B_k}(H)/k >= (n_2-2d_1+k)_2 d_2^2 (1-4p).

nodes.name: Describe backward switching
nodes.statement: A moment of thought (and a glance at Figure~\ref{fig_codegree}) reveals that the backward switching corresponds to choosing a common red neighbor $w_2$ of $u_1$ and $v_1$, choosing alternating cycles $u_1w_2x_1x_2$ and $v_1w_2y_1y_2$ such that $x_1 \neq y_1$ and the edges $v_1x_2$ and $u_1y_2$ are red (note that these assumptions imply $x_2 \neq y_2$), and swapping the colors along the cycles.

nodes.statement_short: Backward switching chooses a common red neighbor and two alternating cycles.

nodes.name: Bounds on backward degree
nodes.statement: Since for every $H' \in {\mathcal{R}}_{k-1}$ the number of choices of $x_2 \in \Gamma_{H'}(u_1) \setminus \Gamma_{H'}(v_1)$ and $ y_2 \in \Gamma_{H'}(v_1) \setminus \Gamma_{H'}(u_1)$ is exactly $(d_1 - k + 1)^2$, we will bound $\deg_{B_k}(H')/(d_1 - k + 1)^2$ from above and below by fixing $x_2, y_2$ and estimating the number of possible triplets $(w_2, x_1,y_1)$. For the upper bound, we can choose~$w_2$ in exactly $\operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus H'}(u_1,u_2) = n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1$ ways, and a pair $x_1, y_1$ of distinct blue neighbors of $w_2$ in at most $(d_2)_2$ ways (we ignore the requirement that $x_1x_2$ and $y_1y_2$ are red). Thus, \begin{equation} \deg_{B_k}(H')/(d_1 - k + 1)^2 \le (n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1)(d_2)_2. \end{equation} For the lower bound, given $x_2, y_2$, we need to subtract from the upper bound \eqref{eq_back_upper} the number of choices of $w_2, x_1, y_1$ for which $x_1x_2$ or $y_1y_2$ is blue. In the former case, ignoring other constraints, there are at most $d_2$ choices of a blue neighbor $x_1$ of $x_2$, at most $d_1$ choices of a blue neighbor $w_2$ of $x_1$, and at most $d_2$ choices of a blue neighbor $y_1$ of $w_2$. By symmetry, the total number of bad choices is at most $2d_1d_2^2$, whence \begin{align*} \deg_{B_k}(H')/(d_1 - k + 1)^2 &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1)(d_2)_2 - 2d_1d_2^2 \\ \justify{$k \ge 1$} &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1)d_2^2\left( 1 - \frac{1}{d_2} - \frac{2d_1}{n_2 - 2d_1} \right) \\ \justify{$d_1 = n_2p, p \le 1/5$} &\ge (n_2 - 2d_1 + k - 1)d_2^2\left( 1- d_2^{-1} - 4p \right). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Case I = 0 (enumeration)
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case $\mathbb I = 0$.} For the switching argument used in the previous case it was crucial that $p$ was small, as otherwise several estimates would be negative and so meaningless. Therefore, it cannot be used now. Fortunately, in this case we are in a position to apply an asymptotic enumeration approach based on Theorem~\ref{thm_enum} and analogous to the proof of Theorem 2.1 in~\cite{KSVW}. Recall the notation ${\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)$ defined before Theorem~\ref{thm_enum}. Writing $A = \Gamma_H(u_1)$ and $B = \Gamma_H(v_1)$, we note that every graph in ${\mathcal{R}}_k$ induces an ordered partition of $V_2$ into four sets $A \cap B$, $A \setminus B$, $B \setminus A$ and $V_2 \setminus (A \cup B)$, of sizes, respectively, $k, d_1 - k, d_1 - k$, and $n_2 - 2d_1 + k$. There are exactly $$\Pi(n_2,d_1,d_2,k):=\frac{n_2!}{k!(d_1 - k)!^2(n_2 - 2d_2 + k)!} $$ such partitions. After removing vertices $u_1$ and $v_1$, we obtain a graph $H^* \in {\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)$ on $(V_1\setminus\{u_1,v_1\}, V_2)$, with $\mathbf{d}_1$ having all its $n_1 - 2$ entries equal to $d_1$, and entries of $\mathbf{d}_2$ determined by the partition: entries equal to $d_2 - 2$ on $A \cap B$, to $d_2 - 1$ on $A \triangle B$ and the remaining ones equal to $d_2$. Since $H^*$ together with the ordered partition uniquely determines $H$, we have \begin{equation*} |{\mathcal{R}}_k| = \Pi(n_2,d_1,d_2,k)\times |{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)|. \end{equation*} Let us check that the three assumptions \ref{thm_enum_max}--\ref{thm_enum_dense} of Theorem~\ref{thm_enum} are satisfied. When doing so, we should remember that we have $n_1 - 2$ instead of $n_1$, but that the parameter $p = d_1/n_2$ remains intact. With foresight, choose $a = 0.35$ and, say, $b = 0.1$, and, for convenience $C = 1$, which determine, via Theorem~\ref{thm_enum}, an $\epsilon > 0$. Note that $\mathbb I = 0$ implies \begin{equation} \hat n \ge \frac{4\max \left\{ n_1,n_2 \right\}} {\log N} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{n_1}{n_2} + \frac{n_2}{n_1} \le \frac{p \log N}{2} \le p \log \max \left\{ n_1, n_2 \right\}. \end{equation} As the degrees on one side are all equal and on the other side they differ from each other by at most $2$, assumption~\ref{thm_enum_max} holds true with a big margin. Using $q \ge 1/2$ and the first inequality in \eqref{eq_p4logN}, we get \[ (pq)^2\min\{n_1 - 2,n_2\}^{1 + \epsilon} \ge \frac{p^2\hat n^{1 + \epsilon}}{4}(1 + o(1)) = \Omega \left( \frac{ \left(\max \left\{ n_1, n_2 \right\}\right)^{1 + \epsilon}}{(\log N)^{3 + \epsilon}} \right) \gg \max \left\{ n_1, n_2 \right\}, \] which implies assumption~\ref{thm_enum_balance} for large $\hat n$. Finally, using elementary inequalities $(1 - 2p)^2 \le q$ (since $p \le 1/2$), $1 \le \left( n_1/n_2 + n_2/n_1 \right)/2$, and the second inequality in \eqref{eq_p4logN}, we obtain \begin{align*} \frac{(1 - 2p)^2}{4pq} &\left(1 + \frac{5(n_1 - 2)}{6n_2} + \frac{5n_2}{6(n_1 - 1)}\right) \le \frac{1}{4p}\left( \frac{1}{2} + \frac{5}{6} \right)\left(\frac{n_1}{n_2} + \frac{n_2}{n_1}\right) (1 + o(1)) \\ &\le \frac{1}{3}\log \max \left\{ n_1, n_2 \right\} (1 + o(1)) \ll 0.35 \cdot \log \max \left\{ n_1 - 2, n_2 \right\}, \end{align*} which for large $\hat n$ implies assumption~\ref{thm_enum_dense} with $a = 0.35$. Note that in \eqref{eq_enum} we have $D_1 = 0$, while $D_2 \le 4n_2 \ll pq n_1n_2$, by the assumption $\hat p\hat n\to\infty$. Thus, uniformly over $k$, the exponent in \eqref{eq_enum} is $-1/2 + o(1)$ and, by Theorem~\ref{thm_enum}, \begin{equation*} |{\mathcal{R}}_k| \sim \frac {e^{-1/2}n_2!\binom {n_2}{d_1}^{n_1 - 2} \binom {n_1 - 2}{d_{2} - 2}^{k}\binom {n_1 - 2}{d_{2} - 1}^{2d_1 - 2k}\binom {n_1 - 2}{d_{2}}^{n_1 - 2d_1 + k}} {k!(d_1 - k)!^2(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)!\binom{(n_1 - 2)n_2}{(n_1 - 2)d_1}} =: r_k. \end{equation*} Straightforward calculations yield \begin{equation*} \frac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} = \frac {(d_1 - k + 1)^2(n_1 - 2 - d_2 + 1)(d_2 - 1)} {k(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)\cdot d_2(n_1 - d_2)} \le \frac{(d_1 - k + 1)^2}{k(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)} \end{equation*} and, because $d_2/n_1 = p\le1/2$, \begin{equation*} \frac{r_k}{r_{k-1}} \ge \frac{(d_1 - k + 1)^2}{k(n_2 - 2d_1 + k)}\left(1 - 2d_2^{-1} \right). \end{equation*} (Compare with \eqref{eq_rkUp} and \eqref{eq_rkLow} to note the absence of $\Theta(p)$ error terms.) With $\mu$ as in \eqref{eq_mu_np_square}, we redefine \begin{equation} \mu_+ := \mu\quad\text{and}\quad\mu_- := \mu (1 - 2d_2^{-1}). \end{equation} From \eqref{eq_mu_np_square} and \eqref{mudef} it follows that \begin{equation} \mu_{+} = \mu \le p^2n_2 (1 + 3d_1^{-1}) \le p^2n_2 + \frac{3pn_2}{n_1}\le p^2n_2 + \frac{20pn_2}{\hat n} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \mu_{-} = p^2n_2 (1 - 2d_2^{-1}) \ge p^2n_2 - 2p \ge p^2n_2 - \frac{20pn_2}{\hat n}. \end{equation} From \eqref{eq_mu_plus} it follows $\mu_+ \le 6p^2n_2$, which implies that $x$ defined in \eqref{eq_def_x} satisfies $x \ge \sqrt{2\mu_+\lambda} + \lambda$. Consequently, using \eqref{eq_mu_plus}, \eqref{eq_mu_minus} and Claim~\ref{clm_Poiss_bounds} we infer \begin{equation*} \prob{|X - p^2n_2| \ge \frac{20pn_2}{\hat n} + x} \le \prob{X \ge \mu_+ + x} + \prob{X\le \mu_- - x} = O\left( \sqrt{N} e^{-\lambda} \right). \end{equation*} We have obtained \eqref{eq_codegconcnoq} in the case $\mathbb I = 0$.

nodes.name: Decompose R_k by partitions
nodes.statement: Recall the notation ${\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)$ defined before Theorem~\ref{thm_enum}. Writing $A = \Gamma_H(u_1)$ and $B = \Gamma_H(v_1)$, we note that every graph in ${\mathcal{R}}_k$ induces an ordered partition of $V_2$ into four sets $A \cap B$, $A \setminus B$, $B \setminus A$ and $V_2 \setminus (A \cup B)$, of sizes, respectively, $k, d_1 - k, d_1 - k$, and $n_2 - 2d_1 + k$. There are exactly $$\Pi(n_2,d_1,d_2,k):=\frac{n_2!}{k!(d_1 - k)!^2(n_2 - 2d_2 + k)!} $$ such partitions. After removing vertices $u_1$ and $v_1$, we obtain a graph $H^* \in {\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)$ on $(V_1\setminus\{u_1,v_1\}, V_2)$, with $\mathbf{d}_1$ having all its $n_1 - 2$ entries equal to $d_1$, and entries of $\mathbf{d}_2$ determined by the partition: entries equal to $d_2 - 2$ on $A \cap B$, to $d_2 - 1$ on $A \triangle B$ and the remaining ones equal to $d_2$. Since $H^*$ together with the ordered partition uniquely determines $H$, we have \begin{equation*} |{\mathcal{R}}_k| = \Pi(n_2,d_1,d_2,k)\times |{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{d}_1,\mathbf{d}_2)|. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: Fix $t < t_0$ and $v\in V_i$ and set $X_t(v) := \deg_{\mathbb R \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v)$. For any $H \in {\mathcal{R}}(n_1,n_2,p)$, conditioning on $\mathbb R = H$, the random variable $X_t(v) \sim \operatorname{Hyp}(M, d_i, M - t)$ has a hypergeometric distribution. Since the distribution does not depend on $H$, $X_t(v)$ has the same distribution unconditionally. In view of \eqref{eq_tau}, $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}} X_t(v) = \tau d_i$, therefore combining \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} and \eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}, for all $x > 0$, \begin{multline} \prob{|X_t(v) - \tau d_i| \ge x} \le 2 \exp \left\{ - \frac{x^2}{2\left(\tau d_i + x/3 \right)} \right\}= 2 \exp \left\{ - \frac{x^2}{2\tau d_i\left(1 + x/(3\tau d_i) \right)} \right\}. \end{multline} Let $x := 3\sqrt{\lambda\tau d_i}$. Since $\tau \ge \tau_0$, by the assumption $\lambda\le \tau_0 p\hat n $, \begin{equation} x/(3\tau d_i) = \sqrt{\lambda/(\tau d_i)} \le \sqrt{\tau_0 \hat n p/(\tau_0 d_i)} \le 1. \end{equation} Consequently, taking the union bound over all $(1 - \tau_0)Mn_i \le N^2$ choices of $t$ and $v$ and using \eqref{Xtv_bound} and \eqref{eq_xtau}, we conclude that \eqref{eq_degupper} fails with probability at most \begin{equation*} 2N^2\exp \left\{ - \frac{x^2}{2\tau d_i\left(1 + x/(3\tau d_i) \right)} \right\} \le 2N^2\exp \left\{ -\frac{9 \tau d_i \lambda}{4\tau d_i} \right\} = 2N^2e^{-9\lambda/4}. \end{equation*}

Fix $t \le M, u_1 
eq v_1$ and let $Y := \left| \Gamma_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1) \cap \Gamma_{H}(v_1)ight|$ and $\operatorname{cod}_H := \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1)$. The distribution of $Y$ conditioned on $\mathbb R = H$ is hypergeometric $\operatorname{Hyp}(M, \operatorname{cod}_H, t)$, and hence, by~\eqref{eq_codHconc}, \[ \mu_Y := \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_H{Y} =  rac{t\operatorname{cod}_H}{M} = (1 - 	au) \operatorname{cod}_H \le (1 - 	au)p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 12 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \] Using \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp}, a trivial bound $\mu_Y \le n_2$, and our assumption $\lambda < n_2$, \[ \probH{ Y \ge \mu_Y + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}} \le \exp\left\{- rac{\lambda n_2}{2(\mu_Y + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}/3)}ight\} \le e^{-3\lambda/8}\le e^{-\lambda/3}. \] Since also trivially $Y \le \min\{d_1, t\}$, we have shown that given $\mathbb R = H$, with probability at least $1 - e^{-\lambda/3}$,  egin{equation} Y \le y_0 := \min \{\mu_Y + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}, d_1, t\} \le (1 - 	au)p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 13 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation} Let ${\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}$ be the event that the inequality in \eqref{enough} holds. By the law of total probability,  egin{align*} \probH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}} &= \sum_y \PcH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}}{Y = y}\probH{Y = y} \ \justify{\eqref{eq_Y}} &\le \sum_{y \le y_0}\PcH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}}{Y = y}\probH{Y = y} + e^{-\lambda/3}. \end{align*} Hence, to prove \eqref{enough}, it suffices to show that, for any $ y = 0, \dots, y_0$,  egin{equation} \PcH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}}{Y = y} \le e^{-\lambda/3}. \end{equation} Fix an integer $y \in [0, y_0]$ and a set $S\subseteq V_2$ of size $|S| = y \le y_0$. Under an additional condi\-tioning $\Gamma_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1)\cap \Gamma_H(v_1) = S$, set $\mathbb R(t)$ is the union of a fixed $y$-element set $\{u_1w : w \in S\}$ and a random $(t - y)$-element subset of $E(H) \setminus \{u_1w : w \in \Gamma_H(u_1)\cap \Gamma_H(v_1)\}$. Thus, in this conditional space, $X := \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1,v_1)$ counts how many of these $t-y$ random edges fall into the set $\{v_1w : w \in S\}$ and therefore $X \sim \operatorname{Hyp}(M - \operatorname{cod}_H, y, t - y)$. Moreover, the distribution of $X$ is the same for all $S$ of size $y$, so $X$ has the same distribution when conditioned on $Y = y$. In particular,  egin{align*} \mu_X := \EcH{X}{Y = y} &=  rac{y(t-y)}{M-\operatorname{cod}_H} \ \justify{$y \ge 0$} &\le  rac{yt}{M} \left(1 +  rac{\operatorname{cod}_H}{M - \operatorname{cod}_H}ight) \ \justify{$M = pn_1n_2, \operatorname{cod}_H \le pn_2$} &\le (1-	au) y \left(1 +  rac{1}{n_1 - 1}ight) \ \justify{$y \le y_0$ and \eqref{eq_Y}} &\le (1-	au)^2p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 13 \sqrt{\lambda n_2} +  rac{n_2}{n_1 - 1}. \ \justify{$n_1 \ge n_2$} &\le (1-	au)^2p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 14 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{align*} Using again \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} as well as inequalities $\mu_X \le n_2$ and $\lambda \le n_2$, we infer that  egin{align*} \PcH{X \ge \mu_X + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}}{Y = y} \le \exp\left\{- rac{\lambda n_2}{2(\mu_X + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}/3)}ight\} \le e^{-\lambda/3} , \end{align*} which, together with the above upper bound on $\mu_X$, implies \eqref{enougher}. This completes the proof of Lemma~ef{lem_codegsRt}.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on R=H with concentrated co-degrees (Lemma 11) and apply two nested hypergeometric tail bounds.

nodes.name: Trivial case
nodes.statement: If $\lambda \ge n_2$, inequality \eqref{eq_codegsRt} holds trivially, so let us assume $\lambda < n_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume lambda < n_2.

nodes.name: Condition on good H
nodes.statement: We can condition on $\mathbb R = H$ satisfying \begin{align} \notag \forall u_1,v_1 \in V_1 \quad\operatorname{cod}_{H}(u_1,v_1) & \le p^2n_2+ 20\left(\hat p^3n_2\mathbb I + n_2\hat p/\hat n + \sqrt{\hat p^2\lambda n_2}\right) + \lambda\\ \notag \justify{$\hat p \le \min \{q, 0.5\}, n_2 = \hat n$}&\le p^2n_2+ 20\left(q^3n_2\mathbb I + 0.5 + 0.5\sqrt{\lambda n_2}\right) + \lambda\\ \justify{$1 \ll \lambda < n_2$} &\le p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 12\sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{align} Indeed, the probability of the opposite event can be bounded, by Lemma~\ref{lem_codegs} and the union bound, by $O\left(n_1^2\sqrt Ne^{-\lambda}\right) \ll N^3e^{-\lambda}$. Taking this bound into account, it thus suffices to show that if $H$ satisfies \eqref{eq_codHconc}, then for any distinct $u_1, v_1\in V_1$ and $t \le M$ \begin{equation} \probH{\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1,v_1) > (1 - \tau)^2p^2 n_{2} + 20 q^3n_2\mathbb I + 15\sqrt{\lambda n_{2}}} = 2e^{-\lambda/3}, \end{equation} since then the proof is completed by a union bound over $O(N^3)$ choices of $t, u_1, v_1$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 11 condition on H with concentrated co-degrees; suffices to prove eq enough.

nodes.name: Co-degree bound on H
nodes.statement: \notag \forall u_1,v_1 \in V_1 \quad\operatorname{cod}_{H}(u_1,v_1) & \le p^2n_2+ 20\left(\hat p^3n_2\mathbb I + n_2\hat p/\hat n + \sqrt{\hat p^2\lambda n_2}\right) + \lambda\\ \notag \justify{$\hat p \le \min \{q, 0.5\}, n_2 = \hat n$}&\le p^2n_2+ 20\left(q^3n_2\mathbb I + 0.5 + 0.5\sqrt{\lambda n_2}\right) + \lambda\\ \justify{$1 \ll \lambda < n_2$} &\le p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 12\sqrt{\lambda n_2}.
nodes.label: eq_codHconc

nodes.name: Conditional co-degree tail bound given R=H
nodes.statement: \probH{\operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1,v_1) > (1 - \tau)^2p^2 n_{2} + 20 q^3n_2\mathbb I + 15\sqrt{\lambda n_{2}}} = 2e^{-\lambda/3},
nodes.label: enough

nodes.name: Bound Y
nodes.statement: Fix $t \le M, u_1 \neq v_1$ and let $Y := \left| \Gamma_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1) \cap \Gamma_{H}(v_1)\right|$ and $\operatorname{cod}_H := \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1)$. The distribution of $Y$ conditioned on $\mathbb R = H$ is hypergeometric $\operatorname{Hyp}(M, \operatorname{cod}_H, t)$, and hence, by~\eqref{eq_codHconc}, \[ \mu_Y := \operatorname{\mathbb{E}}_H{Y} = \frac{t\operatorname{cod}_H}{M} = (1 - \tau) \operatorname{cod}_H \le (1 - \tau)p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 12 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \] Using \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp}, a trivial bound $\mu_Y \le n_2$, and our assumption $\lambda < n_2$, \[ \probH{ Y \ge \mu_Y + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}} \le \exp\left\{-\frac{\lambda n_2}{2(\mu_Y + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}/3)}\right\} \le e^{-3\lambda/8}\le e^{-\lambda/3}. \] Since also trivially $Y \le \min\{d_1, t\}$, we have shown that given $\mathbb R = H$, with probability at least $1 - e^{-\lambda/3}$, \begin{equation} Y \le y_0 := \min \{\mu_Y + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}, d_1, t\} \le (1 - \tau)p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 13 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Y is hypergeometric; Chernoff gives Y <= y_0.

nodes.name: Upper bound on Y
nodes.statement: Y \le y_0 := \min \{\mu_Y + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}, d_1, t\} \le (1 - \tau)p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 13 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}.
nodes.label: eq_Y

nodes.name: Reduce to conditioning on Y=y
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}$ be the event that the inequality in \eqref{enough} holds. By the law of total probability, \begin{align*} \probH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}} &= \sum_y \PcH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}}{Y = y}\probH{Y = y} \\ \justify{\eqref{eq_Y}} &\le \sum_{y \le y_0}\PcH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}}{Y = y}\probH{Y = y} + e^{-\lambda/3}. \end{align*} Hence, to prove \eqref{enough}, it suffices to show that, for any $ y = 0, \dots, y_0$, \begin{equation} \PcH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}}{Y = y} \le e^{-\lambda/3}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By total probability it suffices to prove enougher.

nodes.name: Conditional bound given Y=y
nodes.statement: \PcH{{\mathcal{E}}_\eqref{enough}}{Y = y} \le e^{-\lambda/3}.
nodes.label: enougher

nodes.name: Conditional distribution of X
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $y \in [0, y_0]$ and a set $S\subseteq V_2$ of size $|S| = y \le y_0$. Under an additional condi\-tioning $\Gamma_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1)\cap \Gamma_H(v_1) = S$, set $\mathbb R(t)$ is the union of a fixed $y$-element set $\{u_1w : w \in S\}$ and a random $(t - y)$-element subset of $E(H) \setminus \{u_1w : w \in \Gamma_H(u_1)\cap \Gamma_H(v_1)\}$. Thus, in this conditional space, $X := \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u_1,v_1)$ counts how many of these $t-y$ random edges fall into the set $\{v_1w : w \in S\}$ and therefore $X \sim \operatorname{Hyp}(M - \operatorname{cod}_H, y, t - y)$. Moreover, the distribution of $X$ is the same for all $S$ of size $y$, so $X$ has the same distribution when conditioned on $Y = y$. In particular, \begin{align*} \mu_X := \EcH{X}{Y = y} &= \frac{y(t-y)}{M-\operatorname{cod}_H} \\ \justify{$y \ge 0$} &\le \frac{yt}{M} \left(1 + \frac{\operatorname{cod}_H}{M - \operatorname{cod}_H}\right) \\ \justify{$M = pn_1n_2, \operatorname{cod}_H \le pn_2$} &\le (1-\tau) y \left(1 + \frac{1}{n_1 - 1}\right) \\ \justify{$y \le y_0$ and \eqref{eq_Y}} &\le (1-\tau)^2p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 13 \sqrt{\lambda n_2} + \frac{n_2}{n_1 - 1}. \\ \justify{$n_1 \ge n_2$} &\le (1-\tau)^2p^2n_2 + 20q^3n_2 \mathbb I + 14 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Given Y=y, X is Hyp(M-cod_H, y, t-y); bound its mean.

nodes.name: Chernoff for X
nodes.statement: Using again \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp} as well as inequalities $\mu_X \le n_2$ and $\lambda \le n_2$, we infer that \begin{align*} \PcH{X \ge \mu_X + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}}{Y = y} \le \exp\left\{-\frac{\lambda n_2}{2(\mu_X + \sqrt{\lambda n_2}/3)}\right\} \le e^{-\lambda/3} , \end{align*} which, together with the above upper bound on $\mu_X$, implies \eqref{enougher}. This completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem_codegsRt}.
nodes.statement_short: Upper tail bound gives enougher.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement:
Recall the definitions of $	au=	au(t)$ in \eqref{eq_tau}, $\delta(t)$ in \eqref{eq_deltat}, and $\lambda(t)$ in~\eqref{eq_lambda}. In this proof we utilize some technical bounds on $	au:=	au(t)$ and $\gamma_t$ proved in Section~ef{sec_technical} (see Proposition ef{tech}). In particular, the bound \eqref{eq_gammat_less1} on $\gamma_t$, together with \eqref{eq_deltat_gammat}, implies that  egin{equation} \delta(t) \le 1/9\le 1. \end{equation} (We do not even need to remember what $\gamma_t$ is to see that.) We now derive an upper bound on $\lambda(t)$. By \eqref{eq_taupn}, with a huge margin, \[ 6 \log N \le  rac{	au \hat p \hat n}{16(C + 3)} \le  rac{	au pq\hat n }{8(C+3)}. \] On the other hand, for $p > 0.49$, squaring and rearranging the inequality \eqref{eq_tauq_lower} implies  egin{equation*}  rac{64\log N}{	au p q} \le  rac{	au pq\hat n }{8(C+3)}. \end{equation*} Summing up, for any $p$,  egin{equation} \lambda(t)\le  rac{	au pq \hat n}{4(C + 3)}. \end{equation} Without loss of generality, we assume that $i = 1$. Let ${\mathcal{F}}_t$ be the family of graphs $H$ satisfying, for any distinct $u_1, v_1 \in V_1$,  egin{equation} |d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1) - pqn_2| \le 20\hat p n_{2} \left(\hat p^2\mathbb I +  rac{1}{\hat n} + \sqrt{ rac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{n_{2}}} +  rac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{20\hat pn_2}ight). \end{equation} Lemma~ef{lem_codegs} with $\lambda = (C+3)\lambda(t)$ and a union bound over the $O(N^2)$ choices of $u_1, v_1$ imply  egin{equation} \prob{\mathbb R \in {\mathcal{F}}_t} = 1 - O(N^{2.5} e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}) \By{\lambda(t) \ge 6\log n}{\ge} 1 - O(N^{-(C+1)}e^{-2\lambda(t)}). \end{equation} Writing $\delta_* = \sqrt{ rac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{	au p q \hat n}}$ and noting that \eqref{eq_lambda_upper} implies $\delta_* \le 1/2$, the sum of the last three terms in the parentheses in \eqref{eq_Sienkiewicz} is at most  egin{equation*} 2 \cdot \sqrt{ rac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{\hat n}} +  rac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{20\hat p \hat n} {\le} 2\sqrt{pq}\delta_* +  rac{pq\delta_*^2}{20\hat p} {\le} (1 + 1/40) \delta_*\le  rac{3\delta_*}{\sqrt{6}}. \end{equation*} In addition, the factor in front of the brackets is at most $40pq n_2$. Thus, \eqref{eq_Sienkiewicz} implies  egin{equation} |d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1) - pqn_2| \le 40 pqn_2 \left( \hat p^2 \mathbb I +  rac{3\delta_*}{\sqrt{6}} ight) = pqn_2 \cdot \delta(t)/3. \end{equation} We claim that for $t = 0, \dots, t_0 - 1$  egin{equation} \max_{H \in {\mathcal{F}}_t}\probH{\max_{u_1 
e v_1} \left| rac{	heta_t(u_1,v_1)}{	au pqn_2 } - 1ight| \ge \delta(t)} \le 2N^2e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}, \end{equation} and deferring its proof to the end we first show how \eqref{eq_good_codegs} and \eqref{eq_worst_tail} imply the lemma. Inequalities \eqref{eq_worst_tail} and \eqref{eq_good_codegs} imply  egin{align} 
otag \prob{\max_{u_1 
e v_1} \left| rac{	heta_t(u_1,v_1)}{	au pqn_2 } - 1ight| \ge \delta(t)} &\le 2N^2e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)} + \prob{\mathbb R 
otin {\mathcal{F}}_t} \ &= O(N^{-(C+1)}e^{-2\lambda(t))}). \end{align} Consider random variables, for $t = 0, \dots, t_0 - 1$, \[ Y_t := \Pc{\max_{u_1 
e v_1} \left| rac{	heta_t(u_1,v_1)}{	au pqn_2 } - 1ight| > \delta(t)}{\mathbb R(t)}. \] Using Markov's inequality and \eqref{eq_Epit}, we infer that  egin{align*} \prob{Y_t > e^{-2\lambda(t)}} &\le e^{2\lambda(t)}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}} Y_t = e^{2\lambda(t)}\prob{\max_{u_1 
e v_1} \left| rac{	heta_t(u_1,v_1)}{	au pqn_2 } - 1ight| \ge \delta(t)} = O( N^{-(C+1)}), \end{align*} which, taking the union bound over the $O(N)$ choices of $t$, implies that \eqref{eq_condthetas} holds with the desired probability, completing the proof of lemma. \smallskip Returning to the proof of \eqref{eq_worst_tail}, fix $t < t_0, H \in {\mathcal{F}}_t$ and two distinct vertices $u_1,v_1\in V_1$. Conditioning on $\mathbb R = H$, note that from \eqref{eq_theta_t} that random variable $X := 	heta_t(u_1,v_1) = |\Gamma_{H \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u_i)\cap\Gamma_{K\setminus H}(v_i)|$ counts elements in the intersection of two subsets of $E(H)$: a fixed set $ \left\{ (u_i,w) : w \in \Gamma_H(u_i) \cap \Gamma_{K \setminus H}(v_i) ight\}$ of size $d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1)$ and a random set $H \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ of size $M - t$. Hence $X \sim \operatorname{Hyp}(M, d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1), M -t)$ has the hypergeometric distribution with expectation  egin{equation*} \mu_X := \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} X = (d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1))(M - t)/M = 	au (d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1)). \end{equation*} Note that by \eqref{eq_Tuwim},  egin{equation} |\mu_X - 	au p q n_2| \le 	au pqn_2 \cdot \delta(t)/3. \end{equation} Let $\lambda^* := (3C + 9)\lambda(t)$. From \eqref{eq_theta_exp}, \eqref{eq_delta_upper}, and \eqref{eq_lambda_upper} it follows that  egin{equation} \mu_X \ge  rac{26}{27}	au pqn_{2} \ge \lambda^*. \end{equation} Note that \eqref{eq_deltat} implies  egin{equation} \delta(t)^2\ge7200 rac{\lambda^*}{	au pqn_2}\ge 10 rac{\lambda^*}{	au pqn_2}. \end{equation} By \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp}, \eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}, and \eqref{eq_muHlower},  egin{equation*}  egin{split} \probH{|X - \mu_X| \ge \sqrt{\mu_X \lambda^*} } &\le 2 \exp \left\{ -  rac{\lambda^*}{2\left(1 +  rac{1}{3}\sqrt{\lambda^*/\mu_X } ight)} ight\} \ &\le 2 e^{-3\lambda^*/8}\le 2 e^{-\lambda^*/3} = 2e^{-(C + 3)\lambda(t)}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Thus, with probability $1 - 2e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}$  egin{align*} |	heta_t(u_1,v_1) - 	au p q n_2| &\le |X - \mu_X| + |\mu_X - 	au p q n_2| \ &\le \sqrt{\mu_X \lambda^*} + |\mu_X - 	au p q n_2| \ \justify{\eqref{eq_theta_exp}, \eqref{eq_deltasquared}} &\le \sqrt{\left( 1 + \delta(t)/3 ight)	au p q n_2 \cdot \delta^2(t)	au p q n_2 / 10} + (\delta(t)/3) 	au p q n_2\ \justify{\eqref{eq_delta_upper}} &\le \delta(t)	au pqn_2 (\sqrt{(1 + 1/27)/10} + 1/3) \ &\le \delta(t)	au pqn_2. \end{align*} Hence, applying also the union bound over all $n_1^2 \le N^2$ choices of $u_1,v_1$, we infer \eqref{eq_worst_tail}.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to graphs H with concentrated co-degrees (Lemma 11); theta_t is hypergeometric given R=H, so Chernoff and Markov give the conditional bound.

nodes.name: Recall bounds
nodes.statement: Recall the definitions of $\tau=\tau(t)$ in \eqref{eq_tau}, $\delta(t)$ in \eqref{eq_deltat}, and $\lambda(t)$ in~\eqref{eq_lambda}. In this proof we utilize some technical bounds on $\tau:=\tau(t)$ and $\gamma_t$ proved in Section~\ref{sec_technical} (see Proposition \ref{tech}). In particular, the bound \eqref{eq_gammat_less1} on $\gamma_t$, together with \eqref{eq_deltat_gammat}, implies that \begin{equation} \delta(t) \le 1/9\le 1. \end{equation} (We do not even need to remember what $\gamma_t$ is to see that.)
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 23 gives delta(t) <= 1/9.

nodes.name: delta(t) <= 1/9
nodes.statement: \delta(t) \le 1/9\le 1.
nodes.label: eq_delta_upper

nodes.name: Upper bound on lambda(t)
nodes.statement: We now derive an upper bound on $\lambda(t)$. By \eqref{eq_taupn}, with a huge margin, \[ 6 \log N \le \frac{\tau \hat p \hat n}{16(C + 3)} \le \frac{\tau pq\hat n }{8(C+3)}. \] On the other hand, for $p > 0.49$, squaring and rearranging the inequality \eqref{eq_tauq_lower} implies \begin{equation*} \frac{64\log N}{\tau p q} \le \frac{\tau pq\hat n }{8(C+3)}. \end{equation*} Summing up, for any $p$, \begin{equation} \lambda(t)\le \frac{\tau pq \hat n}{4(C + 3)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: lambda(t) <= tau pq n-hat/(4(C+3)).

nodes.name: Upper bound on lambda(t)
nodes.statement: \lambda(t)\le \frac{\tau pq \hat n}{4(C + 3)}.
nodes.label: eq_lambda_upper

nodes.name: Define F_t
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that $i = 1$. Let ${\mathcal{F}}_t$ be the family of graphs $H$ satisfying, for any distinct $u_1, v_1 \in V_1$, \begin{equation} |d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1) - pqn_2| \le 20\hat p n_{2} \left(\hat p^2\mathbb I + \frac{1}{\hat n} + \sqrt{\frac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{n_{2}}} + \frac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{20\hat pn_2}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: WLOG i=1; F_t = graphs with concentrated co-degrees.

nodes.name: Family F_t condition
nodes.statement: |d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1) - pqn_2| \le 20\hat p n_{2} \left(\hat p^2\mathbb I + \frac{1}{\hat n} + \sqrt{\frac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{n_{2}}} + \frac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{20\hat pn_2}\right).
nodes.label: eq_Sienkiewicz

nodes.name: R in F_t w.h.p.
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem_codegs} with $\lambda = (C+3)\lambda(t)$ and a union bound over the $O(N^2)$ choices of $u_1, v_1$ imply \begin{equation} \prob{\mathbb R \in {\mathcal{F}}_t} = 1 - O(N^{2.5} e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}) \By{\lambda(t) \ge 6\log n}{\ge} 1 - O(N^{-(C+1)}e^{-2\lambda(t)}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 11 and a union bound.

nodes.name: R in F_t with high probability
nodes.statement: \prob{\mathbb R \in {\mathcal{F}}_t} = 1 - O(N^{2.5} e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}) \By{\lambda(t) \ge 6\log n}{\ge} 1 - O(N^{-(C+1)}e^{-2\lambda(t)}).
nodes.label: eq_good_codegs

nodes.name: Simplify the F_t condition
nodes.statement: Writing $\delta_* = \sqrt{\frac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{\tau p q \hat n}}$ and noting that \eqref{eq_lambda_upper} implies $\delta_* \le 1/2$, the sum of the last three terms in the parentheses in \eqref{eq_Sienkiewicz} is at most \begin{equation*} 2 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{\hat n}} + \frac{(C+3)\lambda(t)}{20\hat p \hat n} {\le} 2\sqrt{pq}\delta_* + \frac{pq\delta_*^2}{20\hat p} {\le} (1 + 1/40) \delta_*\le \frac{3\delta_*}{\sqrt{6}}. \end{equation*} In addition, the factor in front of the brackets is at most $40pq n_2$. Thus, \eqref{eq_Sienkiewicz} implies \begin{equation} |d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1) - pqn_2| \le 40 pqn_2 \left( \hat p^2 \mathbb I + \frac{3\delta_*}{\sqrt{6}} \right) = pqn_2 \cdot \delta(t)/3. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: F_t condition implies deviation <= pq n_2 delta(t)/3.

nodes.name: Simplified F_t bound
nodes.statement: |d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1) - pqn_2| \le 40 pqn_2 \left( \hat p^2 \mathbb I + \frac{3\delta_*}{\sqrt{6}} \right) = pqn_2 \cdot \delta(t)/3.
nodes.label: eq_Tuwim

nodes.name: State worst-case tail bound
nodes.statement: We claim that for $t = 0, \dots, t_0 - 1$ \begin{equation} \max_{H \in {\mathcal{F}}_t}\probH{\max_{u_1 \ne v_1} \left|\frac{\theta_t(u_1,v_1)}{\tau pqn_2 } - 1\right| \ge \delta(t)} \le 2N^2e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}, \end{equation} and deferring its proof to the end we first show how \eqref{eq_good_codegs} and \eqref{eq_worst_tail} imply the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Claim eq_worst_tail, proved at the end.

nodes.name: Worst-case tail of theta_t over F_t
nodes.statement: \max_{H \in {\mathcal{F}}_t}\probH{\max_{u_1 \ne v_1} \left|\frac{\theta_t(u_1,v_1)}{\tau pqn_2 } - 1\right| \ge \delta(t)} \le 2N^2e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)},
nodes.label: eq_worst_tail

nodes.name: Markov's inequality
nodes.statement: Consider random variables, for $t = 0, \dots, t_0 - 1$, \[ Y_t := \Pc{\max_{u_1 \ne v_1} \left|\frac{\theta_t(u_1,v_1)}{\tau pqn_2 } - 1\right| > \delta(t)}{\mathbb R(t)}. \] Using Markov's inequality and \eqref{eq_Epit}, we infer that \begin{align*} \prob{Y_t > e^{-2\lambda(t)}} &\le e^{2\lambda(t)}\operatorname{\mathbb{E}} Y_t = e^{2\lambda(t)}\prob{\max_{u_1 \ne v_1} \left|\frac{\theta_t(u_1,v_1)}{\tau pqn_2 } - 1\right| \ge \delta(t)} = O( N^{-(C+1)}), \end{align*} which, taking the union bound over the $O(N)$ choices of $t$, implies that \eqref{eq_condthetas} holds with the desired probability, completing the proof of lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Markov on Y_t and a union bound over t give eq_condthetas.

nodes.name: Prove eq_worst_tail
nodes.statement: Returning to the proof of \eqref{eq_worst_tail}, fix $t < t_0, H \in {\mathcal{F}}_t$ and two distinct vertices $u_1,v_1\in V_1$. Conditioning on $\mathbb R = H$, note that from \eqref{eq_theta_t} that random variable $X := \theta_t(u_1,v_1) = |\Gamma_{H \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u_i)\cap\Gamma_{K\setminus H}(v_i)|$ counts elements in the intersection of two subsets of $E(H)$: a fixed set $ \left\{ (u_i,w) : w \in \Gamma_H(u_i) \cap \Gamma_{K \setminus H}(v_i) \right\}$ of size $d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1)$ and a random set $H \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ of size $M - t$. Hence $X \sim \operatorname{Hyp}(M, d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1), M -t)$ has the hypergeometric distribution with expectation \begin{equation*} \mu_X := \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} X = (d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1))(M - t)/M = \tau (d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1)). \end{equation*} Note that by \eqref{eq_Tuwim}, \begin{equation} |\mu_X - \tau p q n_2| \le \tau pqn_2 \cdot \delta(t)/3. \end{equation} Let $\lambda^* := (3C + 9)\lambda(t)$. From \eqref{eq_theta_exp}, \eqref{eq_delta_upper}, and \eqref{eq_lambda_upper} it follows that \begin{equation} \mu_X \ge \frac{26}{27}\tau pqn_{2} \ge \lambda^*. \end{equation} Note that \eqref{eq_deltat} implies \begin{equation} \delta(t)^2\ge7200\frac{\lambda^*}{\tau pqn_2}\ge 10\frac{\lambda^*}{\tau pqn_2}. \end{equation} By \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp}, \eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}, and \eqref{eq_muHlower}, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \probH{|X - \mu_X| \ge \sqrt{\mu_X \lambda^*} } &\le 2 \exp \left\{ - \frac{\lambda^*}{2\left(1 + \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{\lambda^*/\mu_X } \right)} \right\} \\ &\le 2 e^{-3\lambda^*/8}\le 2 e^{-\lambda^*/3} = 2e^{-(C + 3)\lambda(t)}. \end{split} \end{equation*} Thus, with probability $1 - 2e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}$ \begin{align*} |\theta_t(u_1,v_1) - \tau p q n_2| &\le |X - \mu_X| + |\mu_X - \tau p q n_2| \\ &\le \sqrt{\mu_X \lambda^*} + |\mu_X - \tau p q n_2| \\ \justify{\eqref{eq_theta_exp}, \eqref{eq_deltasquared}} &\le \sqrt{\left( 1 + \delta(t)/3 \right)\tau p q n_2 \cdot \delta^2(t)\tau p q n_2 / 10} + (\delta(t)/3) \tau p q n_2\\ \justify{\eqref{eq_delta_upper}} &\le \delta(t)\tau pqn_2 (\sqrt{(1 + 1/27)/10} + 1/3) \\ &\le \delta(t)\tau pqn_2. \end{align*} Hence, applying also the union bound over all $n_1^2 \le N^2$ choices of $u_1,v_1$, we infer \eqref{eq_worst_tail}.
nodes.statement_short: Given R=H in F_t, theta_t is hypergeometric; Chernoff and union bound.

nodes.name: theta_t is hypergeometric
nodes.statement: Returning to the proof of \eqref{eq_worst_tail}, fix $t < t_0, H \in {\mathcal{F}}_t$ and two distinct vertices $u_1,v_1\in V_1$. Conditioning on $\mathbb R = H$, note that from \eqref{eq_theta_t} that random variable $X := \theta_t(u_1,v_1) = |\Gamma_{H \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u_i)\cap\Gamma_{K\setminus H}(v_i)|$ counts elements in the intersection of two subsets of $E(H)$: a fixed set $ \left\{ (u_i,w) : w \in \Gamma_H(u_i) \cap \Gamma_{K \setminus H}(v_i) \right\}$ of size $d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1, v_1)$ and a random set $H \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ of size $M - t$. Hence $X \sim \operatorname{Hyp}(M, d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1), M -t)$ has the hypergeometric distribution with expectation \begin{equation*} \mu_X := \operatorname{\mathbb{E}} X = (d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1))(M - t)/M = \tau (d_1 - \operatorname{cod}_H(u_1,v_1)). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Given R=H, X = theta_t(u_1,v_1) ~ Hyp(M, d_1-cod_H, M-t).

nodes.name: Mean close to tau pq n_2
nodes.statement: Note that by \eqref{eq_Tuwim}, \begin{equation} |\mu_X - \tau p q n_2| \le \tau pqn_2 \cdot \delta(t)/3. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: eq_theta_exp.

nodes.name: Expectation of theta_t close to tau pq n_2
nodes.statement: |\mu_X - \tau p q n_2| \le \tau pqn_2 \cdot \delta(t)/3.
nodes.label: eq_theta_exp

nodes.name: Lower bounds on mu_X and delta^2
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda^* := (3C + 9)\lambda(t)$. From \eqref{eq_theta_exp}, \eqref{eq_delta_upper}, and \eqref{eq_lambda_upper} it follows that \begin{equation} \mu_X \ge \frac{26}{27}\tau pqn_{2} \ge \lambda^*. \end{equation} Note that \eqref{eq_deltat} implies \begin{equation} \delta(t)^2\ge7200\frac{\lambda^*}{\tau pqn_2}\ge 10\frac{\lambda^*}{\tau pqn_2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: eq_muHlower and eq_deltasquared.

nodes.name: Lower bound on mu_X
nodes.statement: \mu_X \ge \frac{26}{27}\tau pqn_{2} \ge \lambda^*.
nodes.label: eq_muHlower

nodes.name: Lower bound on delta(t)^2
nodes.statement: \delta(t)^2\ge7200\frac{\lambda^*}{\tau pqn_2}\ge 10\frac{\lambda^*}{\tau pqn_2}.
nodes.label: eq_deltasquared

nodes.name: Chernoff
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq_hypergeomUpTailExp}, \eqref{eq_hypergeomLowTailExp}, and \eqref{eq_muHlower}, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} \probH{|X - \mu_X| \ge \sqrt{\mu_X \lambda^*} } &\le 2 \exp \left\{ - \frac{\lambda^*}{2\left(1 + \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{\lambda^*/\mu_X } \right)} \right\} \\ &\le 2 e^{-3\lambda^*/8}\le 2 e^{-\lambda^*/3} = 2e^{-(C + 3)\lambda(t)}. \end{split} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Deviation sqrt(mu_X lambda*) has probability <= 2e^{-(C+3)lambda(t)}.

nodes.name: Conclude eq_worst_tail
nodes.statement: Thus, with probability $1 - 2e^{-(C+3)\lambda(t)}$ \begin{align*} |\theta_t(u_1,v_1) - \tau p q n_2| &\le |X - \mu_X| + |\mu_X - \tau p q n_2| \\ &\le \sqrt{\mu_X \lambda^*} + |\mu_X - \tau p q n_2| \\ \justify{\eqref{eq_theta_exp}, \eqref{eq_deltasquared}} &\le \sqrt{\left( 1 + \delta(t)/3 \right)\tau p q n_2 \cdot \delta^2(t)\tau p q n_2 / 10} + (\delta(t)/3) \tau p q n_2\\ \justify{\eqref{eq_delta_upper}} &\le \delta(t)\tau pqn_2 (\sqrt{(1 + 1/27)/10} + 1/3) \\ &\le \delta(t)\tau pqn_2. \end{align*} Hence, applying also the union bound over all $n_1^2 \le N^2$ choices of $u_1,v_1$, we infer \eqref{eq_worst_tail}.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality and union bound over u_1,v_1.

nodes.name: Edge count e_F(A,B)
nodes.statement: Given a bipartite graph $F \subseteq K$ and two subsets $A \subseteq V_1$, $B \subseteq V_2$, denote by $e_F(A,B)$ the number of edges of $F$ between $A$ and $B$.

nodes.name: (pi,delta)-jumbled graph
nodes.statement: Given real numbers $\pi,\delta\in(0,1)$, we say that a graph $F \subseteq K$ is \emph{$(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled} if for every $A \subseteq V_1$ and $B \subseteq V_2$ \begin{equation*} |e_F(A,B) - \pi|A||B|| \le \delta \sqrt{N|A||B|}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Thomason's jumbledness theorem
nodes.statement: Let $F \subseteq K$ be a bipartite graph and $\rho \in (0,1)$ and $\mu \ge 0$ be given. If \begin{equation} \min_{v \in V_1} \deg_F(v) \ge \rho n_2\quad\text{and}\quad\max_{u,v\in V_1} \operatorname{cod}_F(u,v) \le \rho^2n_2 + \mu, \end{equation} then, for all $A \subseteq V_1$ and $B \subseteq V_2$, \begin{equation*} |e_F(A,B) - \rho|A||B|| \le \sqrt{(\rho n_2 + \mu |A|)|A||B|} + |B|\mathbb I_{\left\{ |A|\rho < 1 \right\}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Minimum degree and maximum co-degree bounds imply edge counts between any A, B are close to rho|A||B|.
assumptions: Let $F \subseteq K$ be a bipartite graph and  $\rho \in (0,1)$ and $\mu \ge 0$ be given.
nodes.label: thm_Thomason

nodes.name: Thomason degree/co-degree hypotheses
nodes.statement: \min_{v \in V_1} \deg_F(v) \ge \rho n_2\quad\text{and}\quad\max_{u,v\in V_1} \operatorname{cod}_F(u,v) \le \rho^2n_2 + \mu,
nodes.label: eq_Thomason_assumption

nodes.name: Thomason's proof carries over to unbalanced bipartite graphs
nodes.statement: \rm The proof in~\cite{T89} is given only in the case $n_1 = n_2 = n$. However, it carries over in this more general setting, as in~\cite{T89} $n$ always refers to $|V_2|$.

nodes.name: Complement of R(t) is jumbled
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha = \min \{ \tau p, q \}$ and $\pi := \tau p + q$. For every constant $C > 0$ and $p > 0.49$, if assumptions \eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} and \eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} hold, then, with probability $1 - O(N^{-C })$, for all $t < t_0$ \begin{equation*} K \setminus \mathbb R(t)\quad \text{is} \quad(\pi, \alpha/16)\text{-jumbled}. \end{equation*} and for any $e \in K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ \begin{equation*} K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{ e \}) \quad \text{is} \quad(\pi, \alpha/16)\text{-jumbled}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: For p>0.49 under the assumptions, w.h.p. for all t<t_0, the complement of R(t) (also minus any edge) is (tau p + q, alpha/16)-jumbled.
assumptions: Let  $\alpha = \min \{ \tau p, q \}$ and $\pi := \tau p + q$.
For every constant $C > 0$ and $p > 0.49$, if assumptions \eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} and \eqref{eq_ef_qlbound} hold
nodes.label: lem_quasiRt

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 17
nodes.statement: W.l.o.g., we assume that $n_1\ge n_2$. Let $\lambda := 3(C + 4)\log N$, and \begin{equation} \delta := 20 \left( \lambda/n_2 \right)^{1/4} + 10q^{3/2}\mathbb I. \end{equation} The plan is to show that \begin{equation} \delta \le \frac{\alpha}{16} \end{equation} and that with the correct probability, $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ and $K \setminus \mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\}$ are in fact $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled. We start with the proof of \eqref{eq_delta_alpha}. Notice that, by \eqref{eq_ef_qlbound}, \begin{equation} \sqrt{\lambda/{n_2}}\le\left(\lambda/{n_2}\right)^{1/4}\le\frac q{680}\le\frac\pi{680}\le\frac1{680}. \end{equation} Since $\hat p > \tfrac{49}{51}q$, condition \eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} implies that $1/320 \ge q^{1/2} \mathbb I$. After multiplying both sides by $10q$, we get \begin{equation*} \frac q{32} \ge 10\cdot q^{3/2} \mathbb I, \end{equation*} which together with the second inequality in \eqref{lnq} implies \begin{equation*} \frac{q}{16} = \frac{q}{32} + \frac{q}{32} \ge 20 \left( \lambda/{n_2} \right)^{1/4} + 10\cdot q^{3/2} \mathbb I = \delta. \end{equation*} On the other hand, using $p > 0.49$, $\tau \ge \tau_0$ and the definition \eqref{eq_tauzero} of $\tau_0$, we infer that \begin{align*} \frac{\tau p}{16} &\ge \frac{0.49 \cdot \tau_0}{16} = \frac{0.49 \cdot 700\cdot (3(C + 4))^{1/4}}{16} \left( \left(\frac{\log N}{n_2}\right)^{1/4} + q^{3/2} \mathbb I\right) \\ &\ge 20 \left( \lambda/{n_2} \right)^{1/4} + 10q^{3/2} \mathbb I = \delta. \end{align*} Hence $\alpha/16 = \min \left\{ \tau p/16, q/16 \right\} \ge \delta$, implying \eqref{eq_delta_alpha}. \smallskip We now prove the jumbledness, first focusing on $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ and then indicating the tiny change in calculation for $K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})$. Fixing an arbitrary $t < t_0$, we will first show that, with probability $1 - O(N^{-C -1})$, conditions \eqref{eq_Thomason_assumption} of Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} are satisfied by $F = K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ and $F = K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})$ for suitably chosen $\rho$ and $\mu$. Then we will apply Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} to deduce that $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ is $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled. Lemma~\ref{lem_quasiRt} will follow by applying the union bound over all (at most $t_0\le M\le N$) choices of $t$. By \eqref{eq_taupn}, $\lambda \le \tau_0 p \hat n$ with a big room to spare. Note that \begin{equation} (1-\tau)p = 1 - \pi, \end{equation} which implies that $|\deg_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v) - \pi n_2|=|\deg_{\mathbb R(t)}(v) - (1-\tau)d_1|$. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem_degrees}, with probability $1 - O(N^2e^{-\lambda})$, \begin{equation} \max_{v \in V_1} |\deg_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v) - \pi n_2| \le 3\sqrt{\tfrac{4}{9}\lambda\tau d_1} \le 2\sqrt{\lambda n_2} \le 3\sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation} Moreover, recalling that $n_1\ge n_2$ and, again using \eqref{pip}, Lemma~\ref{lem_codegsRt} implies that, with probability $1 - O(N^3e^{-\lambda/3})$, \begin{equation} \max_{u, v \in V_1, u \ne v} \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u,v) \le (1 - \pi)^2 n_2 + 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + 15 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation} Since $\lambda = 3(C + 4)\log N$, the intersection of events \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} and \eqref{eq_codeg_Rt} holds with probability $1 - O(N^3e^{-\lambda/3}) = 1 - O(N^{-C - 1})$. Note that for distinct $u, v \in V_1$, by \eqref{eq_coco} and \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} \begin{equation} \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u, v) \le \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u,v) + (2 \pi - 1)n_2 + 6\sqrt{\lambda n_2}, \end{equation} which, by \eqref{eq_codeg_Rt}, implies that \begin{equation} \max_{u, v \in V_1, u \ne v} \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u,v) \le \pi^2 n_2 + 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + (15 + 6) \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation} Set \[ \rho := \pi - 3\sqrt{\lambda/n_2} \quad \text{and} \quad \mu := 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + (15 + 12) n_2\sqrt{\lambda/ n_2}, \] and note that by the inequality $\pi\le1$ and by \eqref{lnq}, we have $0 < \rho < 1$. Furthermore, $\rho^2\ge\pi^2-6\sqrt{\lambda/ n_2}$. Hence, \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} and \eqref{eq_codeg_KRt} imply the assumptions \eqref{eq_Thomason_assumption} for $F = K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ with the above $\rho$ and $\mu$. Consequently, by Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} (using $a \le n_1$ and $\rho\le\pi$), \begin{equation*} |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \rho ab| \le \sqrt{ \left( \pi n_2 + 20q^3n_1n_2\mathbb I + (15 + 12)n_1n_2\sqrt{\lambda /n_2}\right)ab} + b. \end{equation*} Further, since $N=n_1n_2$, $n_1\ge n_2 \ge b$ and $a,\lambda \ge 1$, we have, with a big margin, \[ \pi \le1 \le n_1 \sqrt{\lambda/n_2}\quad\text{and}\quad b \le \sqrt{b n_2} \le \sqrt{Nab}(\lambda/n_2)^{1/4}. \] It follows, applying the inequality $\sqrt{x + y} \le \sqrt x+ \sqrt y$ as well as \eqref{eq_cond_quasiRt}, that \begin{equation} |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \rho ab| \le \left( (\sqrt{15 + 13} + 1)(\lambda/n_2)^{1/4} + \sqrt{20} q^{3/2}\mathbb I\right) \sqrt{Nab} \le \frac{\delta}{2}\sqrt{Nab}. \end{equation} Moreover, note that using $ab \le n_1n_2 = N$ and the first inequality in \eqref{lnq}, \begin{equation} (\pi - \rho)ab = 3\sqrt{\lambda/n_2} \cdot ab \le 3\left(\lambda/n_2\right)^{1/4} \cdot \sqrt{Nab} \le \frac{\delta}{2}\sqrt{Nab}, \end{equation} Hence, \eqref{eq:e_rho} and \eqref{eq:pi_rho} imply \begin{equation*} |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \pi ab| \le |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \rho ab| + (\pi - \rho)ab \le \delta \sqrt{Nab}, \end{equation*} meaning that $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ is $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled. If above we replace $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ by $K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \left\{ e \right\})$, the upper bound in \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} and the bound in \eqref{eq_codeg_KRt} still hold trivially, while the lower bound $\pi n_2 - 3 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}$ in \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} remains correct, since $\deg_{K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})}(v) \ge \deg_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v) - 1$ and we have plenty of room in \eqref{eq_deg_Rt}. Hence Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} applies with the same $\rho$ and $\mu$, implying that $K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})$ is also $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled.
nodes.statement_short: Verify Thomason's degree and co-degree hypotheses for the complement of R(t) via Lemmas 13 and 14, then apply Thomason's theorem.

nodes.name: Set lambda and delta
nodes.statement: W.l.o.g., we assume that $n_1\ge n_2$. Let $\lambda := 3(C + 4)\log N$, and \begin{equation} \delta := 20 \left( \lambda/n_2 \right)^{1/4} + 10q^{3/2}\mathbb I. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Assume n_1 >= n_2; define lambda and delta.

nodes.name: Definition of delta in Lemma 17 proof
nodes.statement: \delta := 20 \left( \lambda/n_2 \right)^{1/4} + 10q^{3/2}\mathbb I.
nodes.label: eq_cond_quasiRt

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: The plan is to show that \begin{equation} \delta \le \frac{\alpha}{16} \end{equation} and that with the correct probability, $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ and $K \setminus \mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\}$ are in fact $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled.
nodes.statement_short: Show delta <= alpha/16 and (pi,delta)-jumbledness.

nodes.name: delta <= alpha/16
nodes.statement: \delta \le \frac{\alpha}{16}
nodes.label: eq_delta_alpha

nodes.name: delta <= alpha/16
nodes.statement: We start with the proof of \eqref{eq_delta_alpha}. Notice that, by \eqref{eq_ef_qlbound}, \begin{equation} \sqrt{\lambda/{n_2}}\le\left(\lambda/{n_2}\right)^{1/4}\le\frac q{680}\le\frac\pi{680}\le\frac1{680}. \end{equation} Since $\hat p > \tfrac{49}{51}q$, condition \eqref{eq_hatpI_ubound} implies that $1/320 \ge q^{1/2} \mathbb I$. After multiplying both sides by $10q$, we get \begin{equation*} \frac q{32} \ge 10\cdot q^{3/2} \mathbb I, \end{equation*} which together with the second inequality in \eqref{lnq} implies \begin{equation*} \frac{q}{16} = \frac{q}{32} + \frac{q}{32} \ge 20 \left( \lambda/{n_2} \right)^{1/4} + 10\cdot q^{3/2} \mathbb I = \delta. \end{equation*} On the other hand, using $p > 0.49$, $\tau \ge \tau_0$ and the definition \eqref{eq_tauzero} of $\tau_0$, we infer that \begin{align*} \frac{\tau p}{16} &\ge \frac{0.49 \cdot \tau_0}{16} = \frac{0.49 \cdot 700\cdot (3(C + 4))^{1/4}}{16} \left( \left(\frac{\log N}{n_2}\right)^{1/4} + q^{3/2} \mathbb I\right) \\ &\ge 20 \left( \lambda/{n_2} \right)^{1/4} + 10q^{3/2} \mathbb I = \delta. \end{align*} Hence $\alpha/16 = \min \left\{ \tau p/16, q/16 \right\} \ge \delta$, implying \eqref{eq_delta_alpha}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare delta with q/16 and tau p/16.

nodes.name: Chain of bounds on lambda/n_2
nodes.statement: \sqrt{\lambda/{n_2}}\le\left(\lambda/{n_2}\right)^{1/4}\le\frac q{680}\le\frac\pi{680}\le\frac1{680}.
nodes.label: lnq

nodes.name: Plan for jumbledness
nodes.statement: We now prove the jumbledness, first focusing on $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ and then indicating the tiny change in calculation for $K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})$. Fixing an arbitrary $t < t_0$, we will first show that, with probability $1 - O(N^{-C -1})$, conditions \eqref{eq_Thomason_assumption} of Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} are satisfied by $F = K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ and $F = K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})$ for suitably chosen $\rho$ and $\mu$. Then we will apply Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} to deduce that $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ is $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled. Lemma~\ref{lem_quasiRt} will follow by applying the union bound over all (at most $t_0\le M\le N$) choices of $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify Thomason's hypotheses for each t, then union bound.

nodes.name: Degrees via Lemma 13
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq_taupn}, $\lambda \le \tau_0 p \hat n$ with a big room to spare. Note that \begin{equation} (1-\tau)p = 1 - \pi, \end{equation} which implies that $|\deg_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v) - \pi n_2|=|\deg_{\mathbb R(t)}(v) - (1-\tau)d_1|$. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lem_degrees}, with probability $1 - O(N^2e^{-\lambda})$, \begin{equation} \max_{v \in V_1} |\deg_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v) - \pi n_2| \le 3\sqrt{\tfrac{4}{9}\lambda\tau d_1} \le 2\sqrt{\lambda n_2} \le 3\sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Degrees of the complement of R(t) are within 3 sqrt(lambda n_2) of pi n_2.

nodes.name: Degree concentration in complement of R(t)
nodes.statement: \max_{v \in V_1} |\deg_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v) - \pi n_2| \le 3\sqrt{\tfrac{4}{9}\lambda\tau d_1} \le 2\sqrt{\lambda n_2} \le 3\sqrt{\lambda n_2}.
nodes.label: eq_deg_Rt

nodes.name: Co-degrees via Lemma 14
nodes.statement: Moreover, recalling that $n_1\ge n_2$ and, again using \eqref{pip}, Lemma~\ref{lem_codegsRt} implies that, with probability $1 - O(N^3e^{-\lambda/3})$, \begin{equation} \max_{u, v \in V_1, u \ne v} \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u,v) \le (1 - \pi)^2 n_2 + 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + 15 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation} Since $\lambda = 3(C + 4)\log N$, the intersection of events \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} and \eqref{eq_codeg_Rt} holds with probability $1 - O(N^3e^{-\lambda/3}) = 1 - O(N^{-C - 1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Co-degrees of R(t) bounded w.h.p.

nodes.name: Co-degree bound in R(t)
nodes.statement: \max_{u, v \in V_1, u \ne v} \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u,v) \le (1 - \pi)^2 n_2 + 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + 15 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}.
nodes.label: eq_codeg_Rt

nodes.name: Co-degrees of the complement
nodes.statement: Note that for distinct $u, v \in V_1$, by \eqref{eq_coco} and \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} \begin{equation} \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u, v) \le \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u,v) + (2 \pi - 1)n_2 + 6\sqrt{\lambda n_2}, \end{equation} which, by \eqref{eq_codeg_Rt}, implies that \begin{equation} \max_{u, v \in V_1, u \ne v} \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u,v) \le \pi^2 n_2 + 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + (15 + 6) \sqrt{\lambda n_2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Co-degrees of the complement are at most pi^2 n_2 + error.

nodes.name: Co-degree of complement via R(t)
nodes.statement: \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u, v) \le \operatorname{cod}_{\mathbb R(t)}(u,v) + (2 \pi - 1)n_2 + 6\sqrt{\lambda n_2},
nodes.label: eq_cod_compl

nodes.name: Co-degree bound in complement of R(t)
nodes.statement: \max_{u, v \in V_1, u \ne v} \operatorname{cod}_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(u,v) \le \pi^2 n_2 + 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + (15 + 6) \sqrt{\lambda n_2}.
nodes.label: eq_codeg_KRt

nodes.name: Apply Thomason
nodes.statement: Set \[ \rho := \pi - 3\sqrt{\lambda/n_2} \quad \text{and} \quad \mu := 20q^3n_2\mathbb I + (15 + 12) n_2\sqrt{\lambda/ n_2}, \] and note that by the inequality $\pi\le1$ and by \eqref{lnq}, we have $0 < \rho < 1$. Furthermore, $\rho^2\ge\pi^2-6\sqrt{\lambda/ n_2}$. Hence, \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} and \eqref{eq_codeg_KRt} imply the assumptions \eqref{eq_Thomason_assumption} for $F = K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ with the above $\rho$ and $\mu$. Consequently, by Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} (using $a \le n_1$ and $\rho\le\pi$), \begin{equation*} |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \rho ab| \le \sqrt{ \left( \pi n_2 + 20q^3n_1n_2\mathbb I + (15 + 12)n_1n_2\sqrt{\lambda /n_2}\right)ab} + b. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Choose rho, mu and apply Theorem 15.

nodes.name: Convert to (pi,delta)-jumbledness
nodes.statement: Further, since $N=n_1n_2$, $n_1\ge n_2 \ge b$ and $a,\lambda \ge 1$, we have, with a big margin, \[ \pi \le1 \le n_1 \sqrt{\lambda/n_2}\quad\text{and}\quad b \le \sqrt{b n_2} \le \sqrt{Nab}(\lambda/n_2)^{1/4}. \] It follows, applying the inequality $\sqrt{x + y} \le \sqrt x+ \sqrt y$ as well as \eqref{eq_cond_quasiRt}, that \begin{equation} |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \rho ab| \le \left( (\sqrt{15 + 13} + 1)(\lambda/n_2)^{1/4} + \sqrt{20} q^{3/2}\mathbb I\right) \sqrt{Nab} \le \frac{\delta}{2}\sqrt{Nab}. \end{equation} Moreover, note that using $ab \le n_1n_2 = N$ and the first inequality in \eqref{lnq}, \begin{equation} (\pi - \rho)ab = 3\sqrt{\lambda/n_2} \cdot ab \le 3\left(\lambda/n_2\right)^{1/4} \cdot \sqrt{Nab} \le \frac{\delta}{2}\sqrt{Nab}, \end{equation} Hence, \eqref{eq:e_rho} and \eqref{eq:pi_rho} imply \begin{equation*} |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \pi ab| \le |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \rho ab| + (\pi - \rho)ab \le \delta \sqrt{Nab}, \end{equation*} meaning that $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ is $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the error terms by delta sqrt(Nab).

nodes.name: Edge count deviation from rho ab
nodes.statement: |e_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(A,B) - \rho ab| \le \left( (\sqrt{15 + 13} + 1)(\lambda/n_2)^{1/4} + \sqrt{20} q^{3/2}\mathbb I\right) \sqrt{Nab} \le \frac{\delta}{2}\sqrt{Nab}.
nodes.label: eq:e_rho

nodes.name: (pi-rho)ab bound
nodes.statement: (\pi - \rho)ab = 3\sqrt{\lambda/n_2} \cdot ab \le 3\left(\lambda/n_2\right)^{1/4} \cdot \sqrt{Nab} \le \frac{\delta}{2}\sqrt{Nab},
nodes.label: eq:pi_rho

nodes.name: Same for the complement minus an edge
nodes.statement: If above we replace $K \setminus \mathbb R(t)$ by $K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \left\{ e \right\})$, the upper bound in \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} and the bound in \eqref{eq_codeg_KRt} still hold trivially, while the lower bound $\pi n_2 - 3 \sqrt{\lambda n_2}$ in \eqref{eq_deg_Rt} remains correct, since $\deg_{K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})}(v) \ge \deg_{K \setminus \mathbb R(t)}(v) - 1$ and we have plenty of room in \eqref{eq_deg_Rt}. Hence Theorem~\ref{thm_Thomason} applies with the same $\rho$ and $\mu$, implying that $K \setminus (\mathbb R(t) \cup \{e\})$ is also $(\pi, \delta)$-jumbled.
nodes.statement_short: The bounds survive removing one edge.

nodes.name: Relative size s(S)
nodes.statement: The {\em relative size} of a subset of vertices $S\subseteq V_i$ is \[ \rs{S} := \frac{|S|}{n_i}. \]
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Relative edge count
nodes.statement: Further, for $X\subseteq V_1$ and $Y\subseteq V_{2}$ and a subgraph $F \subseteq K$, we define \emph{the relative edge count} \[ \varepsilon_F(X,Y) = \varepsilon_F(Y,X) = \frac{e_F(X,Y)}{n_1n_2}. \]
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Relative degree
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $v\in V_i$ and $Y\subseteq V_{3-i}$, we define {\em the relative degree} \[ d_F(v,Y) = \frac{e_F(\left\{ v \right\}, Y)}{n_{3-i}}. \]
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Relative degree d_F(v)
nodes.statement: If $Y = V_{3-i}$, we shorten $d_F(v,Y)$ to $d_F(v)$.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Jumbledness in relative notation
nodes.statement: In this notation, a graph $F$ is $(\pi,\delta)$-jumbled if for every $X \subseteq V_1$, $Y \subseteq V_2$ \begin{equation} |\varepsilon_F(X,Y) - \pi\rs{X}\rs{Y}| \le \delta \sqrt{\rs{X}\rs{Y}}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Jumbledness in relative notation
nodes.statement: |\varepsilon_F(X,Y) - \pi\rs{X}\rs{Y}| \le \delta \sqrt{\rs{X}\rs{Y}}.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs
nodes.label: eq_quasi_rel

nodes.name: Blue and red subgraphs B and R
nodes.statement: Now, let the edges of a graph $F$ be 2-colored by blue and red, and let $B$ and $R$ be the subgraphs of $F$ induced by the edges of color, resp., blue and red.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Blue-red graph
nodes.statement: We then call $F = B \cup R$ \emph{a blue-red graph}.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: (r,b,delta)-regular blue-red graph
nodes.statement: We say that a blue-red graph $F$ is \emph{$(r,b,\delta)$-regular}, if \begin{equation} b - \delta \le d_{B} (v) \le b + \delta, \quad\text{and}\quad r - \delta \le d_{R} (v) \le r + \delta \quad \text{ for every } v\in V_1\cup V_2. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: (r,b,delta)-regularity condition
nodes.statement: b - \delta \le d_{B} (v) \le b + \delta, \quad\text{and}\quad r - \delta \le d_{R} (v) \le r + \delta \quad \text{ for every } v\in V_1\cup V_2.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs
nodes.label: eq_delta_regular

nodes.name: Regularly jumbled graph
nodes.statement: If $F$ is at the same time $(r+b, \delta)$-jumbled and $(r,b,\delta)$-regular, as in the technical lemma below, we will sometimes loosely refer to such a graph as \emph{regularly jumbled}.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Complement S-bar
nodes.statement: Finally, for every $S\subseteq V_i$, $i = 1,2$, set $\overline{S}:=V_i\setminus S$.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs

nodes.name: Technical inequality for regularly jumbled blue-red graphs
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs
nodes.statement_short: In a regularly jumbled blue-red graph, sets X,Y with few blue edges X-to-Ybar and red edges Xbar-to-Y and one small side have both b s(X), r s(Y) at most nu/(1-7 delta/alpha).
assumptions: Let $r, b \in (0,1)$ be real numbers and define $\alpha := \min \{r,b\}$.
let $F \subseteq K$ be a $(r, b, \delta)$-regular, $(b + r, \delta)$-jumbled bipartite blue-red graph
nodes.label: lem_ananas_prep

nodes.name: Small cross edge densities
nodes.statement: \varepsilon_{B}(X,\overline{Y}) + \varepsilon_{R}(\overline{X},Y) \le \nu,
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs
nodes.label: eq_small_cross

nodes.name: min{b s(X), r s(Y)} <= rb/(r+b)
nodes.statement: \min \{b\rs{X},r\rs{Y}\} \leq \frac{rb}{r + b},
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs
nodes.label: eq_less_one

nodes.name: max{b s(X), r s(Y)} bound
nodes.statement: \max \{b\rs{X}, r\rs{Y}\} \le \frac{\nu}{1 - 7\delta/\alpha}.
nodes.section: 6.2 A technical inequality for blue-red graphs
nodes.label: eq_one_smaller

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 18
nodes.statement:
Since \[ \varepsilon_{R}(X,Y) =  rac{e_R(X,Y)}{n_1n_2} =  rac{\sum_{v\in X}e_R(\left\{ v ight\}, Y)}{n_1n_2} =  rac1{n_1}\sum_{v\in X}d_R(v,Y), \] from \eqref{eq_delta_regular} we have  egin{equation} \varepsilon_{R}(X,Y) + \varepsilon_{R}(X,\overline{Y}) \leq (r + \delta)s{X} \end{equation} and, similarly,  egin{equation} \varepsilon_{B}(X,Y) + \varepsilon_{B}(\overline{X},Y) \leq (b + \delta)s{Y}. \end{equation} By summing~\eqref{eq_small_cross},~\eqref{eq_birblue2} and~\eqref{eq_birred2}, we infer that  egin{equation} \varepsilon_F(X,Y) + \varepsilon_F(X,\overline{Y}) + \varepsilon_F(\overline{X},Y)\leq

u + \delta \left(  rac{3x}b +  rac{3y}r +\sqrt{ rac{xy}{br}} ight) =: \psi. \end{equation} Trivially, by the definitions of $s(X)$ and $\alpha$, and by our assumptions on $
